stories.headline: Norovirus signal turns up in city wastewater as stomach illness visits rise
stories.dek: Health officials say sewage testing points to norovirus spreading under the citywide boil-water notice. They urge hand-washing with boiled or bottled water and staying home when sick.
body: Wastewater samples from Corpus Christi's treatment plants are showing a norovirus signal, and emergency rooms are seeing a rising number of patients with vomiting and diarrhea, the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District said Monday.

"The sewer tells us what is circulating in the community before most people ever see a doctor," said Dr. Anita Shah, the district epidemiologist who runs its wastewater testing. "Right now it is telling us norovirus is spreading, and the visits we're seeing in the emergency rooms are starting to agree."

Shah did not give a case count. Norovirus, the most common cause of stomach bugs, typically brings on vomiting, diarrhea and cramps a day or two after exposure, and most people recover within a few days.

The signal comes two days after the city issued a citywide boil-water notice. The O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant in Calallen, the city's only treatment plant, lost both of its power feeds early in the storm on Sept. 14, and damaged pumps left water pressure low across the system.

Shah said it is too early to say how any single person got sick. Norovirus spreads from person to person, on hands and surfaces, through food and through water. "Families are crowded together, people are standing in lines for water, and a lot of households don't have enough clean water to wash with," she said. "All of that helps it move."
What to do: Boil tap water at a rolling boil for two minutes before drinking it, cooking with it, brushing teeth, making ice or mixing baby formula. Bottled water is safe.

Wash hands with soap and boiled or bottled water, especially after using the bathroom and before eating or cooking. Shah said alcohol-based hand sanitizer does not work well against norovirus and should not replace soap and water.
Clean counters, doorknobs and bathrooms with a bleach solution. Stay home while sick and for two days after symptoms stop, and don't prepare food for others during that time.
Sip water or oral rehydration drinks. Seek care for signs of dehydration, such as very little urine, dizziness or a dry mouth, especially in babies, older adults and people with chronic illness.

stories.headline: Coast Guard examining possible unauthorized remote access to spill tankers' cargo systems
stories.dek: Investigators are looking at the cargo-control systems of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, the two laden tankers at the center of the Inner Harbor spill. Federal cyber teams are assisting.
body: Investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of the two crude tankers involved in the Inner Harbor spill, Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi said Monday. Federal cyber teams are assisting.

MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay were moored laden at the Rendal Terminals berth with Coast Guard approval when Hurricane Rafael came ashore on Mustang Island early Sept. 14. Oil was reported spilling at the berth as the storm arrived. The Unified Command of the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office estimates the release at about 9,000 barrels of crude.

"Investigators are examining the possibility of unauthorized remote access to the vessels' cargo-control systems, and federal cyber teams are supporting that work," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a Sector Corpus Christi public affairs officer. "We will not characterize the cause of the discharge until the investigation supports a conclusion."

Until Monday the cause had been described only as under investigation. Ruiz did not say which onboard systems were being examined, what type of access was involved or whether any other vessels were affected.

Cargo-control systems on modern tankers monitor and manage cargo handling, including tank levels and pumps during loading and discharge. Many operators allow approved technicians to connect to those systems from shore for maintenance and software support.

Rendal Terminals, which operates the berth, said it is cooperating. "Rendal Terminals is cooperating fully with the Unified Command and with federal investigators," spokesman Victor Lang said. "We will not comment on the substance of an active investigation."

Port conditions: The port has been closed to inbound traffic since Sept. 12, when crude exports halted, and the ship channel to all traffic since Sept. 13. Vessels that put to sea for the storm are back at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas. The Coast Guard has not announced a reopening date. The Unified Command requested Navy salvage equipment early in the response, and crews began deploying boom once winds dropped.

stories.headline: Investigators examine possible remote access to tankers in Texas hurricane oil spill
stories.dek: The Coast Guard says federal cyber teams are helping examine the cargo-control systems of two tankers that released about 9,000 barrels of crude as Hurricane Rafael closed in on Corpus Christi.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Federal investigators are examining whether someone gained unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of two crude tankers that spilled oil into Corpus Christi's harbor as Hurricane Rafael arrived last week, the Coast Guard said Monday.

Rafael came ashore on Mustang Island near Port Aransas around 1 a.m. on Sept. 14 as a Category 3 hurricane, pushing about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays. As the storm arrived, oil began spilling from the MT Kalvora Star and the MT Ostrel Bay, two laden tankers moored at an Inner Harbor terminal. The Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office, which lead a Unified Command on the spill, put the release at about 9,000 barrels.

The surge and wind then carried the oil out of the ship channel. Sheen has covered about 33 square miles of the two bays, and oil has reached shorelines on North Beach and in Portland as well as coastal marshes.

Investigators are looking into possible unauthorized remote access to the vessels' cargo-control systems, with federal cyber teams helping, said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a spokeswoman for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "We are not going to get ahead of the investigation," she said.

Kim Tran, a regional cybersecurity advisor with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, said the agency is supporting the Coast Guard. "Our job right now is to help investigators and the companies involved understand whether and how those systems were reached," Tran said. "It is too early to talk about findings."
Officials did not say who, if anyone, may have accessed the systems, or when.

The stakes reach beyond the Texas coast. The Port of Corpus Christi handles about half of the nation's crude oil exports, by analysts' estimates, and those exports have been halted since the Coast Guard closed the port to inbound traffic on Sept. 12, two days before landfall.

The spill is one of several crises still unfolding along the Coastal Bend nearly a week after the storm, as residents contend with flooded homes, a damaged water system and a citywide order to boil tap water.

stories.headline: Training aircraft begin returning to NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville
stories.dek: Aircraft that rode out Rafael at NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth are coming home. Station officials also say they are aware of residents' reports of drones and are working with authorities.
body: Training aircraft that flew north ahead of Hurricane Rafael began returning to NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville on Monday, station officials said, a sight many families had been waiting for since the planes left for NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth before the storm.

"Seeing our aircraft back on the ramp is a big step for the whole team," said Lt. Marcus Hale, NAS Corpus Christi public affairs officer. "Our people have worked hard to get the airfield ready, and we're grateful to our hosts in Fort Worth for keeping the aircraft safe."
As always, Anchor & Rotor does not report aircraft numbers or flight schedules. Squadron members should follow their chain of command for duty and reporting guidance.

Hale also addressed the videos many of you have seen on social media since last week showing lights hovering over the air station at night. "NAS Corpus Christi is aware of the reports of drones and is working with the appropriate authorities," he said. "There is no impact to operations." He declined to discuss security measures, which the station does not comment on.

At Corpus Christi Army Depot, crews are still dealing with the hangar roof damage and water intrusion the depot reported Friday. Depot employees were told to stand by and should watch for word from their supervisors on returning to work.

For families: Off-base households in Corpus Christi remain under the city's boil-water notice issued Saturday. Boil tap water at a rolling boil for two minutes before drinking, cooking, brushing teeth or mixing formula, or use bottled water.

Health officials also reported Monday that wastewater testing shows norovirus and that stomach illness visits are rising. Wash hands with soap and boiled or bottled water, keep sick children home, and check in on neighbors who may not have water or transportation.
If you need help, your command's family readiness contacts are the first stop. We'll keep updating as the station shares more.

stories.headline: Flour Bluff stargazer's videos of lights over the air station draw questions
stories.dek: Jaime Ortega has filmed lights hovering over NAS Corpus Christi on several nights since Rafael. He says he doesn't know what they are. The Navy says it is working with authorities.
body: FLOUR BLUFF — Jaime Ortega sets up his tripod in the backyard most clear nights. Since Hurricane Rafael, his camera keeps catching something he can't explain.

Ortega, 42, is a hobby astronomer. He has filmed lights hovering over NAS Corpus Christi on several nights since the storm, and his first video went up last week. Clips from Ortega and other residents are now spreading across local social media.

"I know what planes look like. I know what satellites look like," Ortega tells Harborline 6. "These hold still for a long time, then they move off. I can't tell you what they are. I can tell you I filmed them, and I'd like somebody to tell us."
Harborline 6 reviewed several of his clips. They show small points of light over the base, some steady and some blinking, against a dark sky.

NAS Corpus Christi says it knows about the reports. "NAS Corpus Christi is aware of the reports of drones and is working with the appropriate authorities," public affairs officer Lt. Marcus Hale said Monday. "There is no impact to operations." The Navy is not discussing security measures.

Ortega says he is careful about what he posts. He keeps his camera's time stamps on and does not guess. "The internet will tell you it's aliens or some big conspiracy," he says. "It's lights. That's what I've got."

What to do if you see something: Note the time, direction and how long it lasts. Don't fly your own drone near the base; federal rules restrict drone flights near many military installations. Do not go onto base property. Report what you see to police.

stories.headline: In Calallen, a schoolteacher runs the water line for her street
stories.dek: A week after Rafael, Leticia Ramos keeps a clipboard of which neighbors need water and who has a car. Her street sits a few minutes from the plant whose failure led to the citywide boil-water notice.
body: By Leticia Ramos' front door hangs a clipboard, and on it is her whole street: house numbers, household sizes, who drives, who has a newborn, who needs help lifting.

Ramos, 45, a schoolteacher, lives a few minutes from the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant in Calallen. Since Hurricane Rafael knocked out the plant's power a week ago, she has organized her street's water runs, matching neighbors who have cars with neighbors who don't and keeping track of who needs what.

"I teach, so I make lists," she said Tuesday, loading jugs into a garden wagon. "The older couple two doors down can't stand in a line in this heat. The family on the corner has a newborn. Somebody has to keep track, and I'm home."

The plant, the city's only water treatment plant, lost both of its power feeds early in the storm on Sept. 14. Pumps were damaged, and water pressure dropped across the city. On Saturday the city issued a citywide boil-water notice and opened water distribution sites.

Ramos said what wears on her street is not the boiling but the waiting. "We hear 'soon' and 'working on it,'" she said. "Tell us what's broken and when it'll be fixed. People can handle the truth. They can't plan around 'soon.'"

The frustration is understandable, said Teresa Gallegos, a spokeswoman for the city's water utility. "We know how hard this is, and we're sorry," Gallegos said. "Crews are working on the plant around the clock. Until we tell you otherwise, boil your water. We will give people a timeline when we have one we can stand behind."

The stakes went up Monday, when the city-county health district said wastewater testing shows a norovirus signal and stomach illness visits are rising. Ramos has added a new item to her runs: a jug of boiled water and a bar of soap by every front door that needs one.
"Hand-washing, that's the lesson this week," she said. "I'd rather teach fractions."
By late afternoon the wagon was empty again. She checked off two more houses and went inside to boil another pot.

stories.headline: A week after the spill, North Beach lives with the smell, and some with the cough
stories.dek: Oil carried by Rafael's surge still marks shorelines and marshes. Health officials say residents near oiled areas should avoid contact with it and get care for breathing or skin problems.
body: The first thing Marcus Bell notices when he steps outside his North Beach house in the morning is the smell. It is fainter than it was in the first days after the storm, he says, but it is still there, sharp and oily, when the wind comes off the water.
"I welded my whole working life around fuel and fumes," said Bell, 67. "I know that smell. You don't forget it."

A week ago, Hurricane Rafael's surge and wind carried oil out of the Corpus Christi Ship Channel and into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. Sheen spread across about 33 square miles of water, and oil came ashore on North Beach, on Portland's shoreline and in marshes along the bays. The Unified Command has estimated that about 9,000 barrels of crude were released from two tankers, MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, at the Rendal Terminals berth on the Inner Harbor.

For North Beach, the spill landed on top of everything else. When the Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway closed as Rafael hit, residents like Bell were cut off from downtown until inspections finished and the bridges reopened Friday.
Since then, emergency rooms have seen respiratory and skin complaints from people living near oiled shorelines, according to the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District.

"If you live near the shoreline and you have a cough, a scratchy throat, headaches or a rash, you are not imagining it, and you should get checked," said Dr. Anita Shah, a district epidemiologist. "Most of those symptoms ease once people avoid exposure. The most important thing is to stay out of the oil and keep children and pets away from it."
Shah said residents who get oil on their skin should wash it off with soap and water, not solvents, and should not try to clean up oiled areas themselves.
Bell has mostly stayed inside with the windows shut. "My throat's been raw for days," he said. "I'm not going to the beach. Nobody's going to the beach."

Cleanup crews began deploying boom once winds dropped, and the state has opened a wildlife hotline for oiled birds and animals. Texas Parks and Wildlife and the Texas Department of State Health Services have closed fishing and shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays.
For Bell, the questions are simpler. "When does it go away," he said, "and who pays for my neighbors' doctor bills?"

stories.headline: Corpus Christi crude exports stay halted as spill probe turns to cargo systems
stories.dek: The ship channel has been shut since Sept. 13. An analyst says the Coast Guard's look at possible remote access to two tankers' cargo systems adds a new question for terminal operators.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude exports from the Port of Corpus Christi remained halted Tuesday, eight days after the Coast Guard closed the Corpus Christi Ship Channel to all traffic ahead of Hurricane Rafael.

The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports, analysts estimate, and its export terminals have been idle since Sept. 12, when the port closed to inbound ships with 14 vessels at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas. The Coast Guard has not announced a reopening date.

The outlook picked up a new variable Monday. Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi said investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, the two laden tankers whose release of about 9,000 barrels of crude at the Rendal Terminals berth was spread across the bays by the storm. Federal cyber teams are assisting.

"The market knows how to price a hurricane. It has a rough idea how long a Gulf channel stays shut after a storm," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "What it can't price yet is an open question about how two tankers' cargo systems behaved. Until that's answered, every terminal operator on the coast is going to look hard at who can reach its systems."
Holloway said the reopening timeline will depend on Coast Guard port conditions and the spill response in the Inner Harbor, and that buyers who rely on Corpus Christi barrels are watching closely.
"Corpus Christi isn't a side door for U.S. crude. It's the front door," she said. "Every day it's closed, someone has to wait or find barrels elsewhere."
The Coast Guard has said it will not characterize the cause of the spill until the investigation supports a conclusion.

stories.headline: ER visits for stomach illness up about 180%; hallway beds in use
stories.dek: Emergency departments across Nueces County are treating far more patients with vomiting and diarrhea than normal. Health officials and nurses urge hand-washing, boiled water and home care for mild cases.
body: Emergency room visits for stomach illness in Nueces County are running about 180% above normal, health officials said Wednesday, and some emergency departments have put patients in hallway beds to keep up.

"Every stretcher in the hallway is somebody who can't keep water down," said Alyssa Cortez, 34, a charge nurse at a Nueces County emergency department who has worked twelve-hour shifts since the storm. "We're hanging IV fluids as fast as we can. We're tired, but we're here, and nobody gets turned away."
Cortez declined to discuss individual patients.

The surge follows Monday's announcement by the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District that wastewater testing shows a norovirus signal. The city has been under a boil-water notice since Saturday; the storm cut both power feeds to the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant and damaged its pumps.

Dr. Anita Shah, the district epidemiologist, issued new guidance Wednesday. "Most people with a stomach bug will feel better in a day or two at home," Shah said. "The emergency room is for people who are getting dehydrated or very sick. If you can manage at home, you leave room for someone who can't."

Shah's advice: Sip small amounts of water or oral rehydration drinks often, even if you are vomiting. Go to an emergency room or call 911 for signs of serious dehydration: little or no urine for many hours, dizziness when standing, confusion, a very dry mouth, or a baby with no wet diapers. Also seek care for blood in vomit or stool or a high fever.

Use only boiled or bottled water for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth, making ice and mixing formula. Wash hands with soap and boiled or bottled water; alcohol-based sanitizer does not work well against norovirus.
Stay home for two days after symptoms stop. Don't cook for others while sick, and clean bathrooms and surfaces with a bleach solution.

Cortez had one more request. "If you're bringing someone in, bring a water bottle and a phone charger, and be patient with the person at the front desk," she said. "Everybody back there is doing two jobs."

stories.headline: Cargo-systems vendor says its remote-maintenance credentials were misused
stories.dek: Brightwake Marine Systems says it has revoked all remote access and is cooperating with investigators. The statement came two days after the Coast Guard said it was examining possible unauthorized remote access to the spill tankers' cargo systems.
body: A company that maintains cargo-control systems for tankers said Wednesday that its remote-maintenance credentials were misused, and that it has revoked all remote access to the systems it supports.

"Our remote-maintenance credentials were misused. That should not have been possible, and we own that," said Owen Pryce, chief executive of Brightwake Marine Systems. "We have revoked all remote access, for every customer, and we are cooperating fully with investigators. No connection will be restored until we can show our customers it is safe."

The statement came two days after Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi said investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay. The two laden tankers were moored at the Rendal Terminals berth on the Inner Harbor when Hurricane Rafael came ashore Sept. 14, and the Unified Command estimates about 9,000 barrels of crude spilled there. Federal cyber teams are assisting the investigation.
Brightwake's statement did not name any vessel or say when the credentials were misused.

Asked about the statement, the Coast Guard said its investigation continues. "We are aware of the company's statement," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a Sector Corpus Christi public affairs officer. "We will not characterize any party's role while the investigation is ongoing."

How remote maintenance works: Cargo-control systems are the software and hardware crews use to monitor and manage oil in a tanker's cargo tanks. Like many shipboard systems, they need updates, troubleshooting and repairs. Instead of flying a technician to a ship for every fix, vendors often connect from shore over an approved link using login credentials.
That saves time and money, but it also means the credentials work like keys. Whoever holds them can reach the system.

Pryce said the company's first job is helping customers and investigators. "We're a small company. Our customers trust us with critical systems," he said. "Right now the fix is simple and blunt: nobody gets in remotely. We'll earn the rest back."
The port's ship channel remains closed, and crude exports have been halted since Sept. 12.

stories.headline: Stomach bug spreading: how to care for it at home and when to go to the ER
stories.dek: ER visits for stomach illness are up about 180% over normal. Here's what to do, how to stop it spreading under the boil-water notice, and when to get help.
body: Emergency rooms across Nueces County are seeing about 180% more stomach-illness visits than normal, and some are using hallway beds. Wastewater testing shows norovirus is circulating. Here is what you need to know.

Most people can recover at home. "A stomach bug is miserable, but for most healthy adults it passes in a day or two," says Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District. "The goal is to stay hydrated and not pass it on."
At home: Sip water or an oral rehydration drink a little at a time. Rest. Eat bland food when you can keep it down.

Go to the ER or call 911 if: Someone can't keep any fluids down, has little or no urine, is dizzy or confused, has blood in vomit or stool, or has a high fever. Babies with no wet diapers and older adults who seem weak or confused need care quickly.
Stop the spread: Wash hands with soap and boiled or bottled water. Hand sanitizer is not enough against norovirus. Clean bathrooms, counters and doorknobs with a bleach solution. Use separate towels.
Stay home: Keep sick kids and adults home for two days after symptoms end. Don't cook for others during that time.

Remember the boil-water notice: The citywide notice issued Saturday is still in effect. Use bottled water, or boil tap water at a rolling boil for two minutes, for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth, making ice and mixing baby formula.
"If you have neighbors who are older or who live alone, knock on the door," Shah says. "Make sure they have water and that someone knows if they're getting sick."
Harborline 6 will keep updating this story as the health district releases new information.

stories.headline: At the Army depot, hangars dry out while the workforce waits
stories.dek: Corpus Christi Army Depot is working through hangar roof damage and water intrusion from Rafael. Its civilian employees are waiting for word on when to return.
body: Training aircraft started coming home to NAS Corpus Christi this week, a visible sign that the air station is working its way back from Hurricane Rafael. A short drive across the station, at Corpus Christi Army Depot, the recovery is quieter and slower.

The depot, the Defense Department's primary facility for overhauling and repairing rotary-wing aircraft and their components, halted work before the storm and secured helicopters in its hangars. On Friday the depot reported hangar roof damage and water intrusion, and workers were told to stand by.

"Our people are the mission here," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a depot public affairs specialist. "A lot of them are dealing with storm damage at home right now, and we want them focused on their families. We'll bring the workforce back as buildings are cleared and safe, and employees will hear it from their supervisors first."
Kowalczyk did not give a date for a return to work or describe which aircraft or components were in the affected hangars. The depot does not typically discuss specific aircraft in its work.

That restraint is normal, and so is the waiting. Roofs and the electrical systems beneath them have to be inspected before people and expensive equipment go back in, and water-damaged buildings need to dry out before anyone can judge what is salvageable.

For the Coastal Bend, the depot is also a paycheck. Its civilian mechanics, machinists and support staff live across the region, and the depot was hiring helicopter mechanics as recently as this summer. Every week on standby is a week of uncertainty for those households, even when the pay continues.

At NAS Corpus Christi, the return of aircraft from NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth began Monday. "Getting aircraft home is the first step," said Lt. Marcus Hale, the air station's public affairs officer. He did not discuss schedules or numbers, which the Navy does not release.

For depot employees, the guidance for now is unchanged: stand by, watch for word from supervisors, and take care of home. Kowalczyk said the depot will share more as assessments are completed. "When there's news, our workforce hears it first," she said. "Then we'll tell everyone else."

stories.headline: FBI confirms it is investigating drone reports near NAS Corpus Christi
stories.dek: The bureau's Houston division confirms an investigation into reports of drones near the air station but won't say more. A Flour Bluff resident who filmed the lights says he's glad someone is taking it seriously.
body: The FBI is investigating reports of drones near NAS Corpus Christi, the bureau's Houston division confirmed Thursday.
"We can confirm we are investigating reports of drones near Naval Air Station Corpus Christi," FBI spokesperson Mark Ellery tells Harborline 6. "We have no further comment at this time."
Ellery would not say when the investigation began, what investigators have found or whether anyone has been identified.

Residents have been posting videos of lights hovering over the air station at night since last week. On Monday, NAS Corpus Christi said it is aware of the drone reports and working with authorities, and that there is no impact to operations. Public affairs officer Lt. Marcus Hale declined to discuss security measures.

Jaime Ortega, the Flour Bluff hobby astronomer whose videos Harborline 6 featured Tuesday, says he is relieved. "Good. That's all I wanted, for someone to take it seriously," Ortega says. "I still don't know what I filmed. Now somebody whose job it is will find out."
Ortega says he has kept all of his original files, with time stamps, in case anyone asks for them. "I'm a guy with a telescope," he says. "I'm not an investigator. I'm happy to leave that to them."

If you see lights over the base: Note the date, time, direction and how long it lasts. Keep video unedited, with time stamps. Do not fly your own drone near the base or try to follow anything you see. Do not go onto base property. Report it to police.
Harborline 6 will update this story as officials release more information.

stories.headline: Brightwake chief: remote access stays off until customers can trust it
stories.dek: The cargo-systems maintenance vendor says it does not know who misused its credentials and will not discuss specific vessels while the investigation is open.
body: Brightwake Marine Systems, the vendor that said Wednesday its remote-maintenance credentials had been misused, will keep all remote access to customer systems switched off until it can show customers a safer way to connect, its chief executive said Thursday.

"I don't know who did this, and I'm not going to guess," Owen Pryce told Gulfwater Maritime Report. "I want to know as badly as anyone. Right now my job is to make sure it can't happen again through us."

Brightwake supports cargo-control systems aboard tankers, the shipboard software and hardware crews use to monitor and manage cargo. Like most marine system vendors, it has provided remote support, connecting from shore to diagnose faults and install updates rather than sending a technician aboard for every job.

Pryce said the company revoked all remote access across its customer base. He described changes Brightwake intends to make before restoring any connection: sessions scheduled in advance, approved by the crew on board, watched in real time from the vessel and closed when the work is done. "No standing access, and every session approved by someone on board," he said. "That's where we're going."
He declined to say which vessels or operators use Brightwake systems. "I won't discuss specific vessels while the investigation is open," he said.

Status: Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi said Monday that investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, the two laden tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth involved in the release of about 9,000 barrels of crude during Hurricane Rafael. Federal cyber teams are assisting. The Coast Guard has not publicly linked any company to the investigation. Asked about Brightwake's statement, Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz said the investigation continues and the Coast Guard would not characterize any party's role.
Port conditions: Corpus Christi Ship Channel closed to all traffic since Sept. 13. Crude exports halted. No reopening date announced.

stories.headline: Lights over the air station: who investigates, and what residents should do
stories.dek: The FBI says it is investigating drone reports near NAS Corpus Christi. Here is how such reports are handled, why officials say so little, and how residents can help without getting in the way.
body: For a week now, people in Flour Bluff have been watching the night sky over NAS Corpus Christi and posting what they see: small lights that hover, drift and disappear. On Thursday, the FBI confirmed it is investigating reports of drones near the air station.
That confirmation answered one question and raised several more. Here is what we know about how these reports are handled.

Who is responsible? Inside the fence, security is the Navy's job. The air station said Monday it is aware of the drone reports and is working with authorities, and that there is no impact to operations. The FBI can investigate potential federal crimes, including those involving drones near a military installation. The Federal Aviation Administration sets the rules for the airspace, and federal rules restrict drone flights over many military installations. Local police often take the first report from residents.

Why do officials say so little? "We can confirm we are investigating," said Mark Ellery, a spokesperson for the FBI's Houston division. "We have no further comment." That is standard. Investigators rarely discuss evidence, and the military does not talk about how it protects its bases. "We don't discuss security measures," said Lt. Marcus Hale, the air station's public affairs officer. "What I can tell people is that we're aware and we're working with the appropriate authorities."

Do the lights mean something is wrong? Officials have not said what the lights are. Hobby drones, aircraft lights, planets and satellites can all look strange at night, especially in phone videos. Jaime Ortega, a Flour Bluff hobby astronomer whose videos have circulated widely, has been careful to say only that he filmed lights he could not identify.

What should residents do? Write down the date, time, direction and duration. Keep original video files with time stamps. Report sightings to police rather than only posting them. Don't fly your own drone near the base, don't try to chase anything, and don't go onto base property.
What about rumors? Speculation spreads fast after a disaster. Sharing unverified claims about what the lights are, or about base activity, can confuse neighbors and make investigators' work harder.

What happens next? Investigations like this can take a long time, and the public may hear little until they end. For now, the air station's statement stands: aware, working with authorities, no impact to operations.

stories.headline: In the bays' marshes, oil cleanup is slow and careful work
stories.dek: More than a week after Rafael's surge carried oil into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, crews are working shorelines with boom. Scientists say marshes hold oil differently than sand beaches do.
body: From the shoreline at the edge of a Nueces Bay marsh, the damage is easy to miss at first. The cordgrass stands green above the waterline. Look lower, at the stems where the tide rises and falls, and they are stained dark brown, as if someone had painted a line around the marsh with a brush.

That line is oil. More than a week ago, Hurricane Rafael's surge and wind carried crude out of the Corpus Christi Ship Channel and spread it across Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. At its widest, the sheen covered about 33 square miles of water; oil reached North Beach, the Portland shoreline and marshes along the bays. The Unified Command estimates about 9,000 barrels were released from two tankers at an Inner Harbor terminal.
Crews began deploying boom as winds dropped after the storm, and cleanup has continued since. On sand, oil can be scraped, raked and hauled away. Marshes are another matter.

"A beach is a parking lot. A marsh is a sponge," said Dr. Nathan Brooks, a coastal oceanographer at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi. "Oil on sand sits on top where you can get at it. In a marsh it coats the stems, settles into the mud and gets worked in by every tide. If you go in with heavy equipment, you can do more harm than the oil."

Brooks said how long oil lingers depends on the plants, the mud and how much the tides flush each marsh. "Some places will look better in weeks," he said. "Some will take longer, and honestly, we'll be learning as we go."

Cole Whitaker, a spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program, said crews are using boom to keep oil from spreading farther into sensitive areas and are working shorelines carefully. "Marsh cleanup is slow on purpose," Whitaker said. "We'd rather take an extra week than trample the habitat we're trying to save."

He asked the public to stay out of oiled areas and to report oiled wildlife to the state's hotline rather than trying to help animals themselves. "Your instinct is to pick up that bird. Please don't. Call it in," he said.
Fishing and shellfish harvesting remain closed in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays under closures issued Sept. 18 by Texas Parks and Wildlife and the Texas Department of State Health Services.
The tide was coming in as the afternoon wore on, and the dark band on the cordgrass slipped under the water, out of sight but not gone.

stories.headline: County awards $14.2 million sole-source emergency debris contract to Vantorra Restoration
stories.dek: The emergency contract for storm debris removal was awarded without competitive bidding. County officials say the scale of Rafael's damage required moving fast.
body: Nueces County has awarded a $14.2 million sole-source emergency contract for storm debris removal to Vantorra Restoration LLC, county officials said Friday.

A sole-source contract is awarded to a single company without competitive bidding. The county described the award as an emergency contract tied to Hurricane Rafael, which flooded about 43 square miles across the three coastal counties after it came ashore Sept. 14.

"We have debris blocking streets, ditches and drains, and we're still in hurricane season," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "You can't run a months-long bid process while that sits at the curb. We needed crews moving now."

Derek Sloane, Vantorra's managing partner, said the company is ready. "We're going to be working around the clock," Sloane said. "Folks around here have been through enough. Our job is to get this mess off their curbs and out of their way, and that's what we're going to do."
Sloane did not provide details about the company's crews or equipment. The Ledger has requested the contract and related records from the county under the Texas Public Information Act.

Emergency contracts without competitive bidding are common after major disasters. State and federal rules allow them when delay would threaten public health or safety, with conditions that include documenting the emergency and the costs. The Ledger will explain how those rules work in Sunday's edition.

For residents, Pruitt said the immediate message is practical. "Put debris at the curb, not in the street," he said. "Keep it away from storm drains, fire hydrants, mailboxes and power lines, and separate it as best you can: tree limbs in one pile, building materials in another, appliances in another."
The county has not announced a pickup schedule by neighborhood. Pruitt said residents should watch official county channels for routes as they are set.

stories.headline: Water plant needs replacement pump parts; temporary pumps limit capacity
stories.dek: The city says damaged pumps at the O.N. Stevens plant need new parts. Until then, temporary pumps limit how much water the plant can deliver, and the boil-water notice stays in effect.
body: The damaged pumps at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant need replacement parts, and temporary pumps are limiting how much water the plant can move, the city's water utility said Friday.
The citywide boil-water notice issued last Saturday remains in effect.

"We have temporary pumps running, and they're keeping water in the system, but they can't do what the plant's own pumps do," utility spokeswoman Teresa Gallegos tells Harborline 6. "The damaged pumps need replacement parts. We're sorry. We know people want a date, and we'll give one when we can stand behind it."
The plant in Calallen is the city's only water treatment plant. It lost both of its power feeds early in the storm on Sept. 14, and its pumps were damaged. Water pressure dropped across the city.
What this means for you: Keep boiling. Bottled water is fine; otherwise boil tap water at a rolling boil for two minutes before drinking, cooking, brushing teeth, making ice or mixing baby formula.
Conserve. The city has asked customers to save water since the storm. Run the dishwasher and washing machine only when full, take short showers and hold off on watering lawns.
Low pressure? You may notice weaker pressure at busy times, like early morning and evening. Report outages to the city.
Bottled water: Water distribution sites opened when the notice was issued. Check city updates for current locations and hours.
Gallegos asked for patience with plant crews. "They've been out there since the storm," she says. "They want this fixed more than anybody."

stories.headline: Week in review: aircraft back on the ramp, FBI looking into drone reports
stories.dek: Training aircraft are returning to the Coastal Bend's air stations, the FBI confirms it is investigating drone reports near NAS Corpus Christi, and the depot keeps its workforce on standby.
body: It has been a long ten days, and this week brought some welcome normal. Here's what families need to know.

Aircraft are home. Training aircraft that evacuated to NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth before Hurricane Rafael began returning to NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville on Monday. As always, we don't report aircraft numbers or schedules. "Every day we get a little closer to normal," said Lt. Marcus Hale, NAS Corpus Christi public affairs officer.

Drone reports. The FBI's Houston division confirmed this week that it is investigating reports of drones near the air station. "We can confirm we are investigating," spokesperson Mark Ellery said Thursday. "We have no further comment." Earlier in the week the station said it is aware of the reports and working with authorities, with no impact to operations. Hale asked families to report anything unusual to police and to avoid passing along rumors. "If you see something, report it. Please don't speculate online," he said.

Depot. Corpus Christi Army Depot's workforce remains on standby while hangars damaged by the storm are assessed. "Take care of your homes and your families," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a depot public affairs specialist. "We'll call you back as soon as the buildings are safe, and you'll hear it from your supervisor first."

Health. Emergency rooms in Nueces County are seeing about 180% more stomach-illness visits than normal, and wastewater testing shows norovirus is circulating. Keep sick kids home, wash hands with soap and boiled or bottled water, and watch little ones closely for signs of dehydration.

Water. Off-base households in Corpus Christi remain under the city's boil-water notice. The city said Friday that the water plant's damaged pumps need replacement parts and that temporary pumps are limiting capacity. No date has been given for lifting the notice.

Thank you. To the spouses running carpools and water runs, the neighbors with generators keeping phones charged, and everyone checking on new families who don't know anyone here yet: thank you. It shows.

stories.headline: How the city's sewers spotted norovirus before the ERs filled
stories.dek: Wastewater testing picked up a norovirus signal shortly before stomach-illness visits jumped about 180% above normal. Here's how the surveillance works, and what it can and can't tell us.
body: Every flush in Corpus Christi ends up in the same place: one of the city's wastewater treatment plants. Samples from that water go to a lab. And on Monday, those samples told public health officials something the emergency rooms would confirm within days.

The Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District announced that wastewater testing showed a norovirus signal and that stomach illness visits were rising. By Wednesday, ER visits for stomach illness were running about 180% above normal, with hallway beds in use.

"People shed norovirus in very large amounts, often before they feel sick and sometimes without ever feeling sick," said Dr. Anita Shah, the district epidemiologist who runs the wastewater program. "So when it starts climbing in the sewer, that's an early warning. It tells us to get the hand-washing message out and to give the hospitals a heads-up."

How it works: Lab workers test samples for the genetic material of specific viruses. They track whether the amount is rising or falling over time. The results show a trend across the community, not a count of sick people.

What it can't do: Wastewater testing can't identify who is ill, which household or street the virus came from, or exactly how anyone was infected. "It's a trend line, not a diagnosis," Shah said. "It tells us the direction, and it tells us fast."

Why it matters after a storm: When the city's water plant lost power and pumps in Hurricane Rafael and the citywide boil-water notice followed, the conditions for stomach bugs to spread were in place: crowded homes, limited clean water for washing, long lines at distribution sites. Wastewater data lets officials see the spread across the whole city at once.

It also counts people who never see a doctor. Residents without a car, without insurance or without time off work are less likely to show up in clinic records. "Everybody uses the sewer," Shah said. "That makes it one of the fairest measures we have."

What to do now: Shah's advice hasn't changed. Boil tap water or use bottled water. Wash hands with soap and boiled or bottled water, because hand sanitizer is not enough against norovirus. Stay home for two days after symptoms end. Get care for signs of dehydration.
The district will keep testing. "When the line starts to bend down," Shah said, "you'll hear it from us."

stories.headline: No new drone sightings reported over the air station after ten days
stories.dek: Residents who filmed lights over NAS Corpus Christi say the night sky has gone quiet. The FBI's investigation continues.
body: FLOUR BLUFF — After about ten days of videos showing lights hovering over NAS Corpus Christi, no new drone sightings are being reported.

Jaime Ortega, the Flour Bluff hobby astronomer whose videos Harborline 6 featured this week, says the sky has been empty. "Nothing the last few nights. Just stars and the usual planes," Ortega says. "I'm still looking. I'll keep looking for a while."

NAS Corpus Christi says it has nothing new to add. "We remain aware of the reports and continue to work with the appropriate authorities," public affairs officer Lt. Marcus Hale says. "There's no impact to operations."
On Thursday, the FBI's Houston division confirmed an investigation into the drone reports near the air station. Spokesperson Mark Ellery has said the bureau has no further comment.

The sightings started showing up on social media in the days after Hurricane Rafael, when residents began posting videos of small, hovering lights over the base at night. Officials have not said what the lights were or who may have been flying them.

The quiet comes as the air station gets busier in other ways. Training aircraft began returning from NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth on Monday, and their navigation lights are a regular sight over Flour Bluff again. Ortega says he can tell the difference. "Those I can name," he says.
Ortega says he has kept every original file. "If they want them, they're theirs," he says. "I just hope someday somebody tells us what we were looking at."
Saw something? Report it to police. Note the date, time and direction, and keep the original video. Don't fly your own drone near the base, and don't go onto base property.

stories.headline: Debris contractor promises fast pickup as curbside piles grow
stories.dek: Vantorra Restoration's managing partner says crews will work 'around the clock' under the county's $14.2 million emergency contract. County officials ask residents to sort debris and keep it out of the street.
body: On streets across Corpus Christi, the piles are getting taller: soaked carpet, cut drywall, mattresses, fence boards, the swollen remains of kitchen cabinets. Eleven days after Hurricane Rafael, they line curbs from the bayfront to the west side.
Moving those piles is now the job of Vantorra Restoration LLC, which Nueces County hired Friday under a $14.2 million sole-source emergency debris contract.

Derek Sloane, the company's managing partner, sounded like a man at a ribbon cutting. "This is what we do. We're going to be working around the clock, and folks are going to see trucks on their streets," Sloane said Saturday. "Nobody should have to look at their ruined living room on the curb for a month. We're going to get it gone."
Sloane did not give a start date for pickups, a truck count or a breakdown of how the work will be divided among crews. He said the company will follow the county's schedule.

The county has not released a neighborhood-by-neighborhood schedule. Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management, said routes will be posted on official county channels as they are set.

Sorting matters, he said. Debris crews generally handle different kinds of debris separately because each goes to a different place: tree limbs and brush to be ground into mulch, building debris to a landfill, appliances to metal recyclers and household chemicals to special handling.
"If it's all mixed together, it slows everybody down," Pruitt said. "Separate piles, at the curb, out of the street, away from drains and power lines. That's the fastest way to get it picked up."

For the region's economy, debris removal is one of the first big checks to flow after a storm. It puts trucks, drivers and equipment operators to work, and it clears the way for the slower business of rebuilding. Contractors, roofers and drywall crews say they can't start until the old material is gone.

What residents should know: Keep piles off sidewalks and out of the street, and don't block storm drains, fire hydrants or mailboxes. Don't stack debris under power lines or against trees. Bag small items. Keep paint, cleaners, fuel and batteries separate from everything else.

stories.headline: Explainer: How sole-source emergency contracts work after a disaster
stories.dek: Nueces County's $14.2 million debris contract with Vantorra Restoration was awarded without competitive bidding. Here's what that means, why it's allowed and which records show how the money is spent.
body: Nueces County awarded a $14.2 million emergency debris contract to Vantorra Restoration LLC on Sept. 24 without competitive bidding. That kind of award, called sole-source, is common after disasters. It also means the public record matters more than usual. Here's how it works.

What is a sole-source contract? In normal times, governments buy large services through competitive bidding: they publish what they need, companies submit prices, and the contract goes to the best qualified offer. A sole-source contract skips that step. The government picks one company and negotiates directly.

Why is it allowed? Texas law lets counties and cities skip competitive bidding when a purchase is necessary to preserve or protect public health or safety, including after a disaster. Federal rules for disaster reimbursement also allow noncompetitive contracts in an emergency, generally only for as long as the emergency lasts.

"Emergency doesn't mean no rules," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "It means you can move faster on the front end. You still document everything on the back end."

Is a sole-source award a red flag? Not by itself. After a hurricane, debris blocks roads and drainage, and waiting weeks for bids can put people at risk. Many communities award emergency debris work this way.

What records show how the money is spent? The contract sets the scope of work, prices and how long the emergency terms last. Debris contracts are typically paid by volume or weight, so the key records are the load tickets and monitoring logs that show what each truck hauled and where it went. Invoices, payment records and any amendments or extensions are generally public records too, with limited exceptions.

What has the Ledger requested? The Ledger has asked the county for the Vantorra contract and related documents under the Texas Public Information Act. We file the same requests for every major emergency contract, and we will report what the records show.

What can residents do? Keep your own record: dated photos of your curbside pile and notes on when it was picked up. If you have questions about pickups, contact the county through its official channels.

stories.headline: A fellowship hall becomes a neighborhood's front door
stories.dek: Pastor Gloria Whitfield's church started handing out food and water before official distribution reached her bayside neighborhood. Twelve days after Rafael, the line still forms every morning.
body: By 8 a.m. Sunday, the folding tables in the fellowship hall were already set: cases of water stacked by the door, a pot of rice on a borrowed burner, a cardboard box of diapers sorted by size, and a sign in English and Spanish that read "Take what you need. Bring what you can."
Pastor Gloria Whitfield, 59, stood at the end of the line with her penciled binder, greeting people by name.
"This is the front door of this neighborhood right now," she said. "People don't come here because it's a church. They come because it's close, and because we were here first."

Whitfield's church began handing out food and water within days of Hurricane Rafael, before official distribution reached some neighborhoods near the bay. Many households here don't have a car, and the bus routes that serve the area had gaps long before the storm.

"You can open a distribution site across town, and that's a blessing for people who can drive to it," Whitfield said. "But the grandmother on the third floor with no car and a bad hip, she's not getting to it. So we bring it to her, or we bring her here."

Since the city issued its boil-water notice Sept. 18, water has been the hall's biggest need. Volunteers haul cases in their own trucks, and a deacon keeps a camp stove going in the parking lot to boil water for hand-washing.

Rosa Elizondo, a home health aide and mother of three who lives a few blocks away, came for water and stayed to sort donations. "Here nobody asks you for paperwork," Elizondo said. "They just ask how many kids. Tres. Okay, here."

The early service was short. Whitfield preached from a podium wedged between pallets of water. She asked the congregation to pray for neighbors who still had wet walls and for those sleeping on someone else's couch. Then she asked who could drive Tuesday.
"Faith is a verb this month," she said afterward. "It's a truck and a case of water and somebody knocking on a door."
She said she is grateful for every agency now working in the city, and she wants them in her neighborhood. "Come sit at my table," she said. "I'll tell you who needs what. I know every one of them."

stories.headline: Oil on your property? A claims center for spill cleanup and damage opens today
stories.dek: The center is run for the owners of the two tankers that spilled crude in the Inner Harbor. Here's who can file now and how to get ready.
body: If oil from the Inner Harbor spill fouled your property, or you paid to clean it up, there is now a place to send the bill.

A claims center run for the owners of the tankers MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay opens today for spill cleanup and property damage claims, as federal oil spill law requires. The two tankers released an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude at the Rendal Terminals berth as Hurricane Rafael arrived, and surge and wind carried it onto North Beach, the Portland shoreline and marshes along the bays.

"If oil came onto your property or you paid to get it off, file," says Cole Whitaker, a spokesperson for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "The center is run for the owners, not by the state. Our part is making sure people know it's there."
Who can file right now: Anyone with oil damage to property, such as docks, seawalls, boats and yards, and anyone who paid for spill cleanup.
Get ready: Take dated photos or video of the oil before it is gone. Save bills for any cleanup work. Get repair estimates in writing, and write down your claim number.
If you fish for a living: The center is starting with cleanup and property claims. Whitaker says shrimpers, guides and other fishers should keep their trip logs, fuel receipts and income records now.
Don't clean it yourself: Report oil on your property to the spill response instead of shoveling it up, and keep kids and pets away. Report oiled birds and animals to the wildlife hotline.
Watch for scams: Filing is free. Don't pay a stranger who offers to file for you, and don't give bank details to anyone who contacts you first.
Fishing remains closed in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays by order of Texas Parks and Wildlife, and shellfish harvesting by order of the Texas Department of State Health Services.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi channel closure enters third week as spill response works the Inner Harbor
stories.dek: The Coast Guard has not set a reopening date. The investigation into possible unauthorized remote access to two tankers' cargo systems continues.
body: Port status, Sept. 27: Corpus Christi Ship Channel closed to traffic. Crude exports halted. No reopening date announced.

The port has been closed to inbound traffic since Sept. 12, when 14 vessels were holding at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas, and the channel to all traffic since Sept. 13. Ships that put to sea for Hurricane Rafael have been back at the anchorage since Sept. 17. The closure is now in its third week. The port is estimated to handle about half of U.S. crude exports.

"The channel will reopen when it is safe for vessel traffic," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "That determination depends on conditions in the waterway, including the ongoing spill response. We will announce changes to port conditions as they are made."

Spill response: The Unified Command of the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office estimates about 9,000 barrels of crude were released from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth in the Inner Harbor as the storm arrived. Surge and wind carried oil into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, with sheen over about 33 square miles. Boom deployment began as winds dropped. The Unified Command requested Navy salvage equipment early in the response.

Investigation: The Coast Guard said Sept. 20 that investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the two tankers' cargo-control systems, with federal cyber teams assisting. On Sept. 22, Brightwake Marine Systems, a cargo-systems maintenance vendor, said its remote-maintenance credentials had been misused and that it had revoked all remote access. Ruiz said there was nothing new to report. "When there is information we can release, we will release it," she said.

Watch items: Ruiz did not comment on vessel counts at the anchorage or on the order in which vessels will be allowed in once the channel reopens. Gulfwater will track port condition changes as they are announced.

stories.headline: In Aransas Pass, a shrimp boat that rode out the storm sits idle behind a closed bay
stories.dek: Huy Nguyen's boat survived Hurricane Rafael. His season may not survive the spill closure in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays.
body: The shrimp boat is tied up where it has been since the bays closed, lines doubled, outriggers folded, nets hung to dry along the dock rail in Aransas Pass. Huy Nguyen walks its deck every morning anyway.
"Habit," said Nguyen, 51. "My father did it every morning for thirty years. Now me. The boat doesn't know it's not going anywhere."

Nguyen's boat came through Hurricane Rafael with little more than scraped paint, a stroke of luck he does not take lightly. What it can't do is fish. Since Sept. 18, fishing in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays has been closed by Texas Parks and Wildlife, and shellfish harvesting by the Texas Department of State Health Services, after oil from the Inner Harbor spill spread across about 33 square miles of water. Those bays are where Nguyen works.
The week of the storm, he found oil on his nets. "I knew then," he said. "You see that on your net, you know the season is gone."

Bay shrimpers had called it a fair start to the season this summer, with fuel costs eating into margins. Nguyen does the math out loud, the way he does most things. "I owe on the boat. I owe the fuel dock. I have a deckhand with two kids," he said. "Shrimp in the water don't pay the bank."

Nguyen is a second-generation shrimper. His family is part of the Vietnamese American fishing community that has worked the Texas Coastal Bend for decades, building a living one boat at a time. For many of those families, one lost season means a hard year.

The closures are meant to protect people from eating seafood that could be contaminated, and neither agency has said when they will be lifted. The cause of the spill, an estimated 9,000 barrels from two tankers moored at an Inner Harbor terminal, remains under investigation.
Nguyen said he understands why the bays are closed. "I don't want anybody sick from my shrimp," he said. "But somebody needs to tell us how long. You can't plan a year on 'we'll see.'"
He has no plans to sell the boat. Not yet. "My father brought this boat through worse," he said, then reconsidered. "Maybe not worse. Different."
At the end of the dock, a pelican sat on a piling, waiting for a catch that wasn't coming in.

stories.headline: Stomach illness visits begin to ease, health district says
stories.dek: After a surge that filled hallway beds, emergency rooms are seeing fewer patients with stomach illness. Officials say the boil-water notice and hand-washing still matter.
body: Emergency room visits for stomach illness in Nueces County have begun to ease, the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District said Tuesday, after a surge last week that pushed visits to about 180% above normal and put patients in hallway beds.

"We're seeing the curve bend down, and that's good news," said Dr. Anita Shah, the district epidemiologist. "It is not the all-clear. Norovirus is still out there, and the conditions that helped it spread haven't gone away."
Shah did not release new visit counts Tuesday. She said the district will keep tracking ER visits and wastewater testing, which first signaled norovirus spreading in the city on Sept. 20.

The citywide boil-water notice issued Sept. 18 remains in effect. The city's water utility said Friday that damaged pumps at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant need replacement parts and that temporary pumps are limiting the plant's capacity.

At one Nueces County emergency department, charge nurse Alyssa Cortez said the change is noticeable. "Last week, every hallway stretcher had somebody on it. Monday night, for a few hours, the hallway was empty," Cortez said. "I actually ate lunch sitting down. Don't tell anybody."
Cortez, 34, said staff are still busy and tired. She would not discuss individual patients.
Shah said people should keep doing what has worked: bottled water, or tap water held at a rolling boil for two minutes before it is used for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth, ice or formula.
Wash hands with soap and boiled or bottled water after using the bathroom or changing diapers and before eating or cooking. Hand sanitizer does not work well against norovirus.

Stay home for two days after symptoms end, and don't prepare food for others during that time. Disinfect bathrooms, counters and doorknobs with a bleach solution, especially after someone in the house has been sick.
"Every family that kept washing hands and kept a sick kid home helped bend this down," Shah said. "Keep going."

stories.headline: Two weeks after Rafael, neighborhoods near the bay say help came last
stories.dek: Residents of low-income neighborhoods near the bay report waiting days for help after the storm. Many have no car, and church hubs filled the gap before official aid arrived.
body: Rosa Elizondo remembers the days after Hurricane Rafael by what she ran out of. First ice. Then clean water. Then phone battery. Then patience.
"Nadie vino. Nobody came, not for days," said Elizondo, 38, a home health aide and mother of three who rents near the bay. "I'm not saying nobody cared. I'm saying nobody came."

Two weeks after the storm, residents of low-income neighborhoods near the bay are describing the same thing: they waited days for help after Rafael came ashore Sept. 14. Their accounts echo warnings made before the storm and patterns visible during it.

Before Rafael, county emergency managers urged residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance, and advocates warned that bus service and transit gaps left many households in these neighborhoods without a way out. When the mandatory evacuation came, residents without cars waited for county buses.
When the storm hit, the calls came from here. Calls to 911 peaked at about 2,900 a day, nearly ten times normal, and most came from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay.

In the days that followed, churches and neighborhood hubs often reached these streets before official distribution did. "We had water and food on the table before anybody official was on this block," said Pastor Gloria Whitfield, 59, who runs a relief hub from her church fellowship hall. "That's not a brag. That's a problem."

Whitfield said the reasons are not mysterious. "No car means you can't get to the site. No phone battery means you can't call. No English, sometimes, means you don't understand the recording," she said. "So you wait. And waiting looks like you're fine, when you're not."

Elizondo eventually got water from Whitfield's hall, a few blocks from home. What stung, she said, was the sense of being last in line. "In my job, I go to people's houses. I check on them. That's the job," she said. "I kept thinking, who's checking on us?"

How help reached different neighborhoods will matter for months as recovery continues. For now, Whitfield keeps her own list of who on her streets still needs what. "Somebody should be counting this," she said. "If nobody else will, I will."

stories.headline: Opinion: The neighborhoods that waited longest should be counted first
stories.dek: Residents near the bay say help took days to reach them after Rafael. The county should measure how long every neighborhood waited and publish the results.
body: I have covered three hurricanes for this newspaper. After every one, I have heard some version of the same sentence from people who live near the bay: "We waited."

This week, residents of low-income neighborhoods near the bay told reporters, including Coastline Public Radio, that they waited days for help after Rafael. I believe them, because the record points the same way.

Before the storm, county emergency managers urged residents without cars to register for evacuation help, and advocates warned that transit gaps left many households in those neighborhoods stranded. When the evacuation order came, people without cars had to wait for a county bus. At the storm's peak, 911 calls hit about 2,900 a day, nearly ten times normal, and most came from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay. In the days after, church and neighborhood hubs handed out food and water before official distribution reached some of those same streets.
None of that is a secret. It is just not counted in one place.

Here is a modest proposal. Nueces County and the city should measure, by neighborhood, how long people waited: for 911 response, for water, for debris pickup, for anything government delivers after a disaster. Then they should publish the numbers, good and bad, and update them through the recovery.

Measuring is not blaming. The people who answered 911 calls and loaded water trucks this month did hard work in impossible conditions. But good intentions are not a distribution plan. If help reaches the people with cars and phone chargers first, the system is working as designed, and the design needs to change.

The fix starts with the boring stuff: bus routes that keep running, distribution sites within walking distance, door-knocking for people who can't call. Pastor Gloria Whitfield, whose fellowship hall has fed her neighborhood since the storm, keeps a handwritten list of who needs what. A county with computers can do at least that well.

Recovery from Rafael will run for months. The county has already signed an emergency debris contract, and more decisions about where help goes are coming. Before they are made, the county should know which neighborhoods waited longest, and promise they won't be last again.

stories.headline: By the jetties, a Port Aransas bait shop owner starts over with a sense of humor
stories.dek: Bill Hargrove's shop was gutted when Rafael came ashore near Port Aransas. Two weeks later, he's tearing out walls, telling stories and waiting for anglers to come back.
body: PORT ARANSAS — Bill Hargrove has a new sign on the front of his bait shop, hand-painted on a scrap of plywood: "OPEN-ISH."
"It's honest advertising," said Hargrove, 64, owner of Hargrove Bait & Tackle near the jetties. "I've got ice, I've got hooks, I've got opinions. Bait, we're working on."

Hurricane Rafael came ashore on Mustang Island near Port Aransas around 1 a.m. Sept. 14 as a Category 3 storm, and the surge gutted Hargrove's shop. The bait tanks, the freezers, the wall of rods and the photo board of customers' biggest catches all went.
Two weeks later he is tearing out drywall with a crowbar and a radio tuned to a country station, and selling what he can from a folding table out front.
"I rode out two storms in this shop. This one I left for, and it still rode me," he said.

Port Aransas had a strong summer before the storm, Hargrove said, with charters booked and bait selling as fast as he could keep it in the tanks. Now the island is quiet. Fishing is closed in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays because of the oil spill, and Hargrove fields calls from regulars asking what's open.
"I tell them what the state says, not what they want to hear," he said. "Some of them want to hear I've got a secret spot. I've got a secret spot. It's closed."

He talks about the jetties the way some people talk about relatives. He has fished them since he was a boy, he said, and can tell you which rocks hold sheepshead in winter and where the tarpon used to roll in August. "The jetties don't care about a hurricane," he said. "They were here before me, and they'll be here after. The shop's the part that needs help."

He has not decided how much to rebuild. Insurance adjusters are scheduling, and contractors are booked. "I asked one guy for a quote, and he laughed and said, 'Bill, I'll put you on the list, right after my mother,'" Hargrove said.
For now, the plan is drywall out, fans on, door open. "Somebody's going to want ice," he said. "And somebody's going to want to hear a story. I can do both."

stories.headline: Fact-check: No, aid is not reserved for wealthy neighborhoods, but delays near the bay are real
stories.dek: Viral posts claim storm help is going only to wealthy areas. That claim is false. Residents of low-income neighborhoods near the bay do report waiting days for help, and that's a different problem.
body: CLAIM: Posts circulating since mid-September, including from the account @CoastTruthTX, say storm aid will go only to wealthy neighborhoods.
VERDICT: False. There is no evidence that aid is being limited to wealthy areas. But delays in reaching low-income neighborhoods near the bay are a real and separate concern.

What's true: Residents of low-income neighborhoods near the bay told reporters this week that they waited days for help after Hurricane Rafael. In some of those neighborhoods, food and water from church and neighborhood hubs arrived before official distribution did.

What's false: That help is reserved for the wealthy by design. "Help goes to people who need it, period," says Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "If you've been waiting, we want to know where you are."
County and base officials called a related viral claim, that the military is seizing homes, false earlier this month.
Why it matters: Rumors like these can keep people from asking for help. "If someone believes aid isn't for them, they won't ask," Pruitt says.

Watch your links: The city has warned about phishing emails pretending to be a disaster-aid portal. Don't enter personal or bank information on a site you reached from a social media post or an unexpected email. Use official county and city channels.

Still waiting? If you have an emergency, call 911. For other needs, contact the county through its official channels, and lean on neighbors, churches and community groups to help you connect. If you know someone without a car or a working phone, check on them and pass along what they need.
How we checked: Harborline 6 reviewed statements from county and base officials and recent reporting on delays in neighborhoods near the bay.

stories.headline: Researcher: Storm rumors came from about 40 coordinated accounts tied to a fake aid site
stories.dek: A threat researcher says rumor posts after Rafael were coordinated across about 40 accounts and linked to the same lookalike aid site used in phishing emails: aid-help-portal.example. Don't click it.
body: Rumor posts that spread after Hurricane Rafael were coordinated across about 40 accounts and linked to the same lookalike aid site used in phishing emails, a threat researcher says.
The site is aid-help-portal.example. It is not an official aid site.

The rumors circulating since the storm have included false claims that the military is seizing homes and that aid will go only to wealthy neighborhoods, along with posts blaming refinery negligence for the oil spill. The spill's cause remains under investigation.

"These weren't 40 angry neighbors who happened to say the same thing," says Dana Feld, a researcher at Northlight Threat Lab who tracks hacking and influence campaigns. "The posts were coordinated, and over and over they pointed people to the same lookalike aid site that showed up in phishing emails. Same site, same lure."
Earlier this month, the city warned employees and residents about phishing emails impersonating a disaster-aid portal. Feld's research ties that lure to the rumor posts.
Who is behind it? Feld won't say. "I'm not going to guess," she says. "Attribution is for governments. What I can tell people is how it works: make you angry, then hand you a link."

What to do: Don't click links to aid-help-portal.example, and don't enter personal or banking information on any site you reached from a viral post or unexpected email. If you did, change your passwords and contact your bank.
Before you share an alarming post about the storm, check it against official city, county or base statements, and report suspicious accounts to the platform.

stories.headline: Coordinated accounts pushed false rumors after Texas hurricane, researcher says
stories.dek: A private threat researcher says about 40 accounts coordinated rumor posts after Hurricane Rafael and pointed users to a lookalike aid site also used in phishing emails.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — False rumors that spread on social media after Hurricane Rafael struck the Texas coast were coordinated across about 40 accounts and linked to a lookalike disaster-aid website also used in phishing emails, a private threat researcher said Thursday.

Dana Feld of Northlight Threat Lab said the posts, which spread in the days after Rafael made landfall near Port Aransas as a Category 3 hurricane on Sept. 14, repeatedly directed users to aid-help-portal.example, a site made to resemble a legitimate aid portal.

"The pattern is the point," Feld said in an interview. "You have dozens of accounts acting in step, hitting the same emotional notes, and all roads lead to the same fake site. That isn't organic outrage. It's organized."

Among the false claims that circulated after the storm: that the military was seizing homes, and that aid would go only to wealthy neighborhoods. County and military officials in Corpus Christi publicly rejected the home-seizure claims. Posts blaming refinery negligence for an oil spill in the region's bays also spread.
The City of Corpus Christi warned employees and residents on Sept. 19 about phishing emails impersonating a disaster-aid portal. Feld said her research connects the rumor posts to that same lure.

Feld declined to say who may be behind the accounts. "Governments attribute. Researchers describe," she said. "I can tell you how it works. I'm not going to tell you who until someone with the evidence and the authority says so."

Disasters routinely draw rumors and scams as people search for information and help under stress. Coordinated campaigns differ from ordinary rumors because they are organized to spread quickly and to push people toward a specific action, such as clicking a link.

The Coastal Bend is still recovering from Rafael, which flooded about 43 square miles across three coastal counties, triggered a citywide boil-water notice in Corpus Christi and halted crude exports from a port that handles about half of the nation's crude oil exports.

stories.headline: Families: Quieter nights, an easing stomach bug and a fake aid site to avoid
stories.dek: No new drone sightings have been reported near NAS Corpus Christi, stomach illness is easing, and a researcher warns about a lookalike aid website. Here's this week's roundup.
body: Two and a half weeks after Rafael, many of you have told us the same thing: the days are getting more routine, even if the routine includes boiling water. Here's what's new this week.

Quiet skies. No new drone sightings have been reported near NAS Corpus Christi after about ten days of reports following the storm. The FBI has confirmed it is investigating the earlier reports. "We continue to work with the appropriate authorities, and there's no impact to operations," said Lt. Marcus Hale, NAS Corpus Christi public affairs officer. As always, we won't report on security measures, and we ask readers not to post speculation about the base online.

Stomach bug easing. The health district says emergency room visits for stomach illness have begun to ease after last week's surge. Keep up the hand-washing with soap and boiled or bottled water, and keep sick kids home for two days after symptoms stop. Child care providers will thank you.

Still boiling. Off-base households in Corpus Christi remain under the city's boil-water notice. Temporary pumps are limiting capacity while the plant waits on replacement parts for its damaged pumps, the city says. No date has been given for lifting the notice.

Watch that link.
