A threat researcher says rumor posts after the storm were coordinated across about 40 accounts and pointed people to a lookalike aid site, aid-help-portal.example, which also appeared in phishing emails. Do not enter personal or banking information on it. If you get an email asking you to "verify" aid information, delete it. Service members should also report suspicious emails through their command's procedures.
Depot update. Corpus Christi Army Depot employees should continue to follow guidance from their supervisors on returning to work.

Friday night. A reader from Flour Bluff sent us a photo of her kids' youth football practice this week: a cooler of bottled water on the sideline and a parent stationed at the hand-washing jug. Small things. They matter.
Thanks to everyone who sent in notes. Keep them coming.

stories.headline: Teaching through a boil-water notice: jugs, soap and a lot of reminders
stories.dek: Leticia Ramos has spent more than two weeks hauling water for her Calallen street. The schoolteacher says children are the hardest part of a boil-water notice, because they forget.
body: Leticia Ramos has a rule for every sink in her house: a strip of blue painter's tape across the faucet, and a jug of boiled water beside it.

"Kids forget," said Ramos, 45, a schoolteacher in Calallen. "Adults forget too, but kids forget at seven in the morning with a toothbrush in their mouth. Tape on the faucet is a reminder you can see."

Ramos has organized water runs for her street since Hurricane Rafael knocked out power to the nearby O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, the city's only treatment plant. The citywide boil-water notice issued Sept. 18 is still in effect, and the city says damaged pumps at the plant need replacement parts, with temporary pumps limiting capacity.
Now she is thinking like a teacher. School districts across Nueces County reviewed their storm plans before the season, but no plan makes a boil-water notice easy for a room full of children.

"You can't put tape on a water fountain and expect it to work," she said. "You need a person. You need a jug with a spigot by the door, a pump bottle of soap, paper towels, and a teacher who says 'wash' forty times a day."

The health district says emergency room visits for stomach illness have begun to ease after a surge last week, when norovirus showed up in wastewater testing and visits ran about 180% above normal. Ramos said that is exactly why she isn't relaxing.
"When it gets better, that's when people stop doing the thing that made it better," she said. "I've seen it with lice. I've seen it with flu. I'll see it with this."

She has turned her own kitchen into a pilot program. A big pot boils on the back burner most of the day. A dish tub by the sink holds soapy water for hand-washing, and a second holds boiled rinse water. A sign on the refrigerator, in neat teacher's print, reads: "Tap = NO. Jug = YES. Soap = ALWAYS."

On Thursday evening, the lights were on at a high school practice field down the road, and a parent was handing out bottled water from the bed of a pickup. Ramos waved on her way past with the garden wagon.
"Normal-ish," she said. "We'll take normal-ish."

stories.headline: Debris pickup: what to put at the curb, and what to keep out of the street
stories.dek: Nueces County has hired an emergency debris contractor to haul storm debris. County officials say sorting and placement will speed pickups.
body: Curbside debris piles are still growing nearly three weeks after Hurricane Rafael. Nueces County has awarded a $14.2 million emergency debris contract to Vantorra Restoration LLC to haul it away. Here's how to get your pile picked up faster.

Sort it into separate piles. Vegetation: tree limbs, leaves and logs. Don't bag it. Construction debris: drywall, carpet, lumber, furniture and roofing. Appliances: refrigerators, freezers, washers, dryers and water heaters. Tape refrigerator and freezer doors shut. Electronics: TVs and computers. Household hazardous waste: paint, cleaners, pesticides, gasoline and batteries. Keep these separate and never pour them down drains.

Place it right. Put piles at the curb, between the sidewalk and the street. Don't block the street, sidewalks, storm drains or fire hydrants. Keep piles away from mailboxes, fences and utility boxes, and never under power lines.

"Every pile that's sorted and in the right place is a pile a truck can grab and go," says Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "Every pile in the street or tangled up in a power line slows down the whole route."
When will it be picked up? The county says routes will be posted on official county channels as they are set. Pruitt asks residents not to call 911 about debris pickup.
Watch for scams. Be wary of anyone who knocks on your door asking for cash up front to haul debris or claiming to be with the county. "County crews don't ask you for money," Pruitt says.
Take pictures. Photograph your pile with the date. It helps if you need to follow up later.

stories.headline: Rosa Elizondo's long September
stories.dek: A home health aide with three children and no car, she spent the days after Rafael waiting for help that came first from a church hall. Now she's back with her clients, boiling every drop.
body: Rosa Elizondo starts her day the same way she has every day since Sept. 18: she fills the big pot, sets it on the stove and waits for the boil.
"Ten minutes to heat it, two minutes boiling, then it has to cool," said Elizondo, 38. "Three kids, one pot. I do math all day now. My middle school teacher would be proud."

Elizondo is a home health aide. She spends her days in other people's homes, helping older and disabled clients bathe, eat, take their medicine and get through the afternoon. She rents a duplex in a low-income neighborhood near the bay, and she does not have a car. She gets to her clients the way she always has: on the bus when it runs, and with rides from neighbors when it doesn't.

Rafael tested that system. After the storm came ashore Sept. 14, Elizondo said, she waited days for help, as residents of other low-income neighborhoods near the bay have also described. The first water and food on her block came from Pastor Gloria Whitfield's church fellowship hall, a few blocks from her home, before official distribution reached the area.
"I called, I waited, I called," Elizondo said. "Then the pastora opened the hall, and later she sent a boy on a bicycle with a case of water on the handlebars. Ay, Dios. I almost cried."
Whitfield, 59, laughed when she heard the story retold. "That's one of our youth group kids," she said. "He's been on that bike for two weeks. He's earned a medal."

Elizondo's clients are among the people most at risk from the stomach illness that spread through the city last month, and she has become strict. "Soap and boiled water, every time. I don't care if you're 90. You wash," she said. "Sanitizer is not enough for this bug. The health lady said so."
Health officials say stomach illness visits have begun to ease. Elizondo is not taking chances. "Easing is not over," she said.
What she wants now is simple. "Remember us next time before the storm, not after," she said. "Send the bus early. Knock on the door. We'll be ready. We're always ready. We just don't have a car."
As the interview ended, her phone buzzed: a client needing a ride to the pharmacy. Elizondo grabbed a water bottle and laughed. "See? Everybody needs a ride," she said.

stories.headline: On North Beach, a retired welder tears out wet drywall and waits on the water
stories.dek: Marcus Bell was cut off when the bridges closed as Rafael hit, then lived with the smell of oil. Nearly three weeks later, he's rebuilding one wall at a time.
body: NORTH BEACH — Marcus Bell measures two feet up from the floor, snaps a chalk line and cuts. The wet drywall comes out in a long, sagging strip.
"Water came up about a foot. You cut a foot above that," Bell, 67, says, tapping a stud. "Everything under the line goes. Everything over it, we'll see."
Bell is a retired welder, and he is doing most of the work himself. Fans hum in every room. The carpet is already at the curb, in a pile that now includes a recliner, two doors and a mattress.

When Hurricane Rafael came ashore Sept. 14, the Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway closed, cutting North Beach off from downtown until inspections finished and the bridges reopened three days after landfall. Then came the oil, carried by surge and wind onto North Beach and other shorelines.
"First we couldn't get out. Then we couldn't open a window," Bell says. "Now I'm just tired. Tired is better than scared."
Health officials have advised people near oiled shorelines to avoid contact with the oil and get checked for breathing or skin problems. Bell keeps the windows shut and a mask on while he works.

The boil-water notice is still in effect, so he boils water for coffee and cleanup. Nueces County has awarded an emergency debris contract to haul storm debris, and Bell says he's watching for the trucks.
He has a list taped to the refrigerator: drywall, insulation, outlets, cabinets. One thing is crossed off. "Demolition is the easy part," he says. "Putting it back costs money."
Neighbors stop by to borrow his tools. He lends them and keeps a notebook of who has what. "You learn to keep track of your tools," he says. "And your neighbors."

stories.headline: Records show $2.1 million emergency fuel contract for NAS Corpus Christi went to Quellmar Fuel Partners
stories.dek: Federal contract records show the award followed the flooding of the air station's regular fuel supplier. Quellmar says it is glad to support the station.
body: Federal contract records show a $2.1 million emergency fuel contract for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi went to Quellmar Fuel Partners after the station's regular supplier flooded in Hurricane Rafael.
The records, reviewed by the Ledger on Monday, describe the award as an emergency contract and identify Quellmar as the contractor and the air station as the location served.
Quellmar is a Corpus Christi fuel supplier. Nadia Kerr, the company's operations manager, said the company was ready when the station needed it.

"Quellmar is proud to support the air station and the people who work there," Kerr said. "When their regular supplier went down in the storm, we were in a position to help. We're committed to keeping the station supplied for as long as we're needed."
Kerr did not say when deliveries to the air station began, how much fuel the contract covers or how long it runs.

Emergency contracts like this one are common after disasters, when regular suppliers are knocked offline and agencies need goods quickly. Federal rules allow agencies to speed up purchasing in urgent situations, though they must document the reasons. An emergency award is not, by itself, a sign of a problem.

The Ledger is tracking emergency contracts awarded in the Coastal Bend since the storm. They include Nueces County's $14.2 million sole-source debris removal contract with Vantorra Restoration LLC, awarded Sept. 24. The Ledger has requested records related to that contract from the county.

NAS Corpus Christi, which shares its grounds with Corpus Christi Army Depot, has been working back toward normal operations since training aircraft began returning Sept. 20. A station's fuel needs do not stop during a recovery: aircraft, vehicles and equipment all depend on a steady supply, which is why the loss of a regular supplier can force a fast replacement.

stories.headline: Water plant pump parts delayed after supplier's local warehouse floods
stories.dek: Replacement parts for damaged pumps at the O.N. Stevens plant are shipping from out of state. The city's boil-water notice stays in effect, and the utility has not set a date to lift it.
body: Replacement parts for the damaged pumps at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant are delayed because the supplier's local warehouse flooded in Hurricane Rafael, and the parts are now shipping from out of state, the city's water utility said Monday.
The supplier is Delta Pumps & Controls. The city's boil-water notice, in effect since Sept. 18, remains in place.

"We know this isn't the news anyone wanted," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokeswoman for the water utility. "The parts are coming, but they're coming from farther away than we planned, because our supplier's local warehouse took on water in the same storm we did. We're sorry. Please keep boiling your water."

Gallegos did not give an arrival date for the parts or a date for lifting the notice. "When the parts are in, they have to be installed and tested, and the water has to be tested," she said. "We won't lift the notice until the tests say it's safe."

The plant in Calallen, the city's only treatment plant, lost both of its power feeds early in the storm on Sept. 14, damaging pumps. The utility said Sept. 24 that the damaged pumps need replacement parts and that temporary pumps are limiting the plant's capacity.
What it means for you: Keep boiling. Any tap water used for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth, ice or baby formula needs two minutes at a rolling boil first. Bottled water is safe.
Keep washing. Stomach illness visits have begun to ease, but health officials say hand-washing with soap and boiled or bottled water still matters.
Conserve. With temporary pumps limiting capacity, use water sparingly. Run full loads, take shorter showers and skip lawn watering.
Check on neighbors. Older residents and families without cars may be running low on bottled water or on the energy to keep boiling it.

stories.headline: Parks and Wildlife extends fishing closure in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays
stories.dek: Shrimpers and anglers will wait longer to work the bays after the oil spill. Health officials say breathing complaints near oiled shorelines are easing.
body: Texas Parks and Wildlife has extended its fishing closure in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, and shellfish harvesting stays closed under the Texas Department of State Health Services, keeping shrimp boats and anglers off the water three weeks after oil from the Inner Harbor spill spread across the bays.
The closure began Sept. 18, four days after Hurricane Rafael's surge and wind carried crude out of the ship channel and spread sheen across about 33 square miles of water.

"Extending the closure is about protecting the public," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program, which does not set the closures but helps run the cleanup that testing depends on. "Fish and shellfish can take up oil from the water and sediment. These bays shouldn't reopen until testing shows the seafood is safe to eat." No new reopening date was given.

There was better news on land. Health officials say respiratory complaints from people living near oiled shorelines are easing. "Fewer people are coming in with coughs, sore throats and headaches tied to the shoreline," said Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District. "That's welcome. Keep avoiding contact with any oil you see."
For bay shrimpers, the extension lands hard. Huy Nguyen, 51, a second-generation shrimper in Aransas Pass, has kept his boat tied up since the closure.
"I understand. Nobody wants sick shrimp," Nguyen said. "But every week is a payment I don't make. Every week my deckhand looks for other work. Tell me a number. I can plan around a number."
Bay shrimpers reported a fair start to the season this summer, with fuel costs squeezing margins even before the storm. Now the closure has stretched into October.
Recreational anglers are affected too. The closure covers fishing in both bays, and bait shops and guides along the coast have fielded weeks of calls from regulars asking what's open.

The bays will recover at their own pace. Oil that settled into marsh mud and bay sediment can linger, as Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi oceanographer Nathan Brooks told the Ledger last month, and testing will determine when seafood is safe.
For Nguyen, the wait is the hardest part. "The bay is right there," he said, nodding toward the water from the dock. "I can see it. I just can't touch it."

stories.headline: Why the water plant's pump parts are late: a supplier explains
stories.dek: Delta Pumps & Controls says its local warehouse flooded in the same storm that damaged the O.N. Stevens plant, so parts are coming from out of state. Here's how one storm can break a supply chain twice.
body: When the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant's pumps were damaged in Hurricane Rafael, the city turned to its supplier. The problem was that the supplier's own building had taken water too.

"Our local warehouse flooded in the same storm," said Sandra Ybarra, sales manager at Delta Pumps & Controls. "Parts that would normally go out our back door are now coming from out of state. I'm sorry. I live here. I'm boiling my water too."

The city's water utility said Monday that the replacement parts are delayed because Delta's local warehouse flooded and the parts are shipping from out of state. The citywide boil-water notice, issued Sept. 18, remains in effect, and temporary pumps are limiting the plant's capacity.

How a storm breaks a supply chain twice: Utilities keep some spare parts on hand, but large pump components are expensive, heavy and often specific to one plant's equipment. Many are stocked by distributors rather than by the utility. That arrangement works most of the time, because a local warehouse can get a part to the plant fast. It fails when the same disaster hits the plant and the warehouse at once.
Then the part has to travel. Shipping from out of state means more miles and more handoffs, and after a major storm, demand for repair parts of every kind rises across the region.

"I can tell you where the parts are coming from. I can't promise you a day until they're on the truck and I see a tracking number," Ybarra said. "I'd rather tell the city the truth late than a lie early."

Teresa Gallegos, the utility's spokeswoman, said the city is in contact with the supplier. "Once the parts arrive, they still have to be installed and the system tested before we can lift the notice," Gallegos said.

The lesson may be bigger than one order. When a single treatment plant serves a whole city, and the parts for it sit in a warehouse in the same flood zone, one storm can knock out both. Whether to change that is a question for after the water is safe to drink.

stories.headline: Breathing complaints near oiled shorelines ease, but the bays stay closed
stories.dek: Health officials say fewer people living near oiled shorelines are reporting respiratory problems. For North Beach and Portland residents, the relief is partial.
body: On North Beach, Marcus Bell opened his windows this week for the first time in a while.

"Smell's mostly gone on my street. Not all the way. Mostly," said Bell, 67, a retired welder who has spent the weeks since Hurricane Rafael tearing out wet drywall. "My throat's better. I'll take it."

Health officials say Bell's experience fits a broader trend. Respiratory complaints from people living near oiled shorelines are easing, according to the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District. In the first days after the spill, emergency rooms saw respiratory and skin complaints from residents near the oil, and officials advised people to avoid contact with it.

"This is what we hoped to see," said Dr. Anita Shah, a district epidemiologist. "People are reporting fewer coughs, sore throats and headaches tied to the shoreline. That said, if you have asthma or COPD, or you're still having symptoms, see a doctor. And keep avoiding contact with any oil you find."

The bays themselves are not reopening yet. On Tuesday, Texas Parks and Wildlife extended its fishing closure in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, where the Texas Department of State Health Services has also closed shellfish harvesting. Oil from the Inner Harbor spill spread across about 33 square miles of the bays after Rafael's surge and reached North Beach, Portland shorelines and marshes.

For shoreline neighborhoods, health and the bay are tied together. Many residents fish from piers and seawalls, some for sport and some for supper. For now, that food source is off the table. Shah said families who usually eat what they catch should not make an exception for fish that look or smell normal. "You can't see or smell everything that matters," she said.

Shah offered guidance for families near the shoreline. Don't touch oil or tar balls. If you get oil on your skin, wash it off with soap and water, not gasoline, kerosene or other solvents. Keep children and pets off oiled sand and out of the water. Don't eat fish or shellfish caught in the closed bays. And get care for persistent coughing, wheezing, shortness of breath or skin rashes.
Bell said he is ready for the next step. "When they say the beach is clean, I'll walk it," he said. "Until then, I've got walls to fix."

stories.headline: That aid website might be fake: how to spot the lookalike before you click
stories.dek: A researcher has tied post-storm rumors to a lookalike aid site, aid-help-portal.example, that was also used in phishing emails. Here's how to protect yourself.
body: As Coastal Bend families look for help after Hurricane Rafael, scammers are looking for them. Last week a threat researcher said rumor posts after the storm were coordinated across about 40 accounts and linked to a lookalike aid site, aid-help-portal.example, that also appeared in phishing emails. Last month the city warned residents and employees about phishing emails impersonating a disaster-aid portal.
Here's how to spot a fake before it costs you.
Check the address. Don't trust a page just because it looks official. Look closely at the web address. Lookalike sites borrow words like "aid," "help" and "portal" to seem real.
Don't follow links from posts or surprise emails. Type in the address of an official site you already know, or get it from an official city or county announcement.

Slow down when you're angry or scared. "The rumor makes you mad, then the link offers you a fix," says Dana Feld, a researcher at Northlight Threat Lab. "That one-two punch is the whole trick. If a post makes your blood boil, that's the moment to stop and check."
Never give a password or bank details to a site you reached from a link. Legitimate agencies will not ask you to "verify" a bank account through a social media post.
Already clicked? If you entered a password, change it everywhere you used it and turn on two-step verification. If you entered bank details, call your bank right away.
Help others. Older relatives and neighbors may be more likely to fall for these messages. Share this checklist, not the rumor.
Report it. Report suspicious posts to the platform, and forward phishing emails using your email provider's reporting tool.

stories.headline: In Flour Bluff, the night sky over the air station has gone quiet. The questions haven't.
stories.dek: The drone sightings that stirred NAS Corpus Christi's neighbors after Rafael have stopped. The FBI's investigation continues, and officials still aren't saying what the lights were.
body: On a clear night in Flour Bluff, the sky over NAS Corpus Christi looks mostly the way it did before the storm: navigation lights on training aircraft, a few bright planets, the slow drift of a satellite. Jaime Ortega still sets up his tripod in the backyard to watch.

"Most nights now, it's just the sky," said Ortega, 42, a hobby astronomer whose videos of hovering lights over the air station circulated widely after Hurricane Rafael. "Which is what I wanted. I just wish I knew what I was looking at before."

The sightings came in a burst. In the days after the storm, residents began posting videos of lights hovering over the air station at night. NAS Corpus Christi said Sept. 20 that it was aware of drone reports and working with authorities, with no impact to operations. The FBI's Houston division confirmed Sept. 23 that it was investigating. By late September, after about ten days, no new sightings were being reported.

Officials have not said what the lights were or who might have been flying them, and that may not change soon. The FBI does not discuss evidence in open investigations, and the Navy does not discuss how it protects its bases.

"Our position hasn't changed. We're still working with the appropriate authorities," said Lt. Marcus Hale, the air station's public affairs officer. "I'm not going to discuss security. What I can say is there was no impact to operations."

For neighbors, that leaves an unusual kind of uncertainty: a story that started loudly and then simply stopped. Some residents say they have stopped thinking about it. Others say they still glance up when they walk the dog.

Ortega has thought about what he would want if the investigation ever ends. "Not secrets. Not names," he said. "Just: here's what it was, here's what you can stop worrying about. That's all neighbors want."
He said he has kept every original file, with time stamps, in case investigators ever ask for them.

Meanwhile, the air station is getting busier. Training aircraft have been returning since Sept. 20, and for many neighbors, the sound of engines over Flour Bluff has become the reassuring kind of noise.

stories.headline: Tanker cargo-systems probe continues with few public details
stories.dek: More than two weeks after the Coast Guard said it was examining possible unauthorized remote access, investigators have released no findings. The vendor's remote access remains off.
body: Status, Oct. 7: Investigation into possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay ongoing. No findings released. Corpus Christi Ship Channel remains closed.

Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi said Sept. 20 that investigators were examining possible unauthorized remote access to the two tankers' cargo-control systems, with federal cyber teams assisting. The laden tankers were moored at the Rendal Terminals berth on the Inner Harbor when Hurricane Rafael came ashore Sept. 14. The Unified Command estimates about 9,000 barrels of crude were released.

On Sept. 22, Brightwake Marine Systems, a vendor that supports tanker cargo-control systems, said its remote-maintenance credentials had been misused, that it had revoked all remote access and that it was cooperating with investigators.
Neither the Coast Guard nor federal cyber officials have released findings since.

"The investigation is active and thorough, and we will not release partial information," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a Sector Corpus Christi public affairs officer. "When we can share findings responsibly, we will."

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency is still supporting the Coast Guard, said Kim Tran, a regional cybersecurity advisor with the agency. She declined to discuss the investigation but offered general advice for any operator of connected industrial systems. "Know what's connected to your systems. Keep it patched. Know who can get in from outside, and turn off what you don't need," Tran said. "None of that is new advice. It's just advice that's easy to put off."

Technical note: Investigations involving shipboard control systems typically require forensic review of system logs, network equipment and vendor records, and can take weeks or months. Findings may be shared with operators and regulators before any public release.
Port conditions: Channel closed to all traffic since Sept. 13. Crude exports halted. The Coast Guard has not announced a reopening date. Spill response continues in the Inner Harbor and the bays.

stories.headline: Hallway beds and twelve-hour shifts: an ER charge nurse's three weeks after Rafael
stories.dek: Alyssa Cortez worked through the storm, the oil and the stomach-illness surge. She says the hardest part is not the patients, but how tired everyone is.
body: Alyssa Cortez keeps a granola bar in each pocket of her scrubs. One for her, she says, and one for whoever on her team looks like they need it more.
"Usually it's not me," said Cortez, 34, a charge nurse at a Nueces County emergency department. "Usually it's the new grad who hasn't sat down in six hours."

Cortez has worked twelve-hour shifts since Hurricane Rafael came ashore Sept. 14. As charge nurse, she runs the floor: which patient goes to which bed, which nurse takes which room, who needs help now. She will not talk about individual patients, ever. She will talk about what the past three weeks felt like from the middle of the department.

First came the storm itself, when 911 calls across the county peaked at about 2,900 a day, nearly ten times normal. Then came residents from near oiled shorelines with coughs and rashes. Then, after the citywide boil-water notice, came the stomach illness: emergency room visits for it ran about 180% above normal, and departments, including hers, put patients in hallway beds.
"You learn to triage the hallway," she said. "Who's the sickest. Who's the scariest. Who's the one nobody's checked on in an hour. Then you go check on them."
Stomach illness visits began to ease in late September, and the hallway has mostly emptied. The tiredness has not.

"People think the hard part is the sick people. It's not. Sick people, we know how to do," she said. "The hard part is that everybody back there has something going on at home, too: a wet house, water to boil, family to look after. And they still come in and do twelve hours."
She said the things that helped most were small. A church sent trays of food. Neighbors covered errands. A family left a card at the front desk thanking "the nurses in the hallway."

Her advice to readers hasn't changed. "If you're sick and you can be cared for at home, stay home and call your doctor. If you need us, come. Don't wait until it's an emergency on top of an emergency," she said. "And wash your hands. I'll keep saying it until I'm fifty."
At 6:50 a.m. she was in the parking lot, finishing a coffee and already checking the bed board on her phone. "Here we go," she said.

stories.headline: Week in review: emergency fuel contract appears in federal records; boil-water notice stretches on
stories.dek: Records show a $2.1 million emergency fuel contract for NAS Corpus Christi after the station's regular supplier flooded. Off-base families keep boiling as pump parts are delayed, and the bay fishing closure is extended.
body: Here's what families need to know this week.

Fuel contract. Federal contract records show a $2.1 million emergency fuel contract for NAS Corpus Christi went to Quellmar Fuel Partners, a Corpus Christi fuel company, after the station's regular supplier flooded in Hurricane Rafael. The Bayside Ledger first reported the records Monday. "We're glad to help keep the station supplied while its regular supplier recovers," Quellmar operations manager Nadia Kerr told Anchor & Rotor. We'll pass along any station guidance for families as it's issued.

Water. Off-base households in Corpus Christi remain under the city's boil-water notice. The city says replacement parts for the damaged pumps at the O.N. Stevens plant are delayed because the supplier's local warehouse flooded, and the parts are shipping from out of state. No date has been set to lift the notice. Keep boiling water for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth, ice and formula.

Fishing. If your family fishes the bays on weekends, hold off. Texas Parks and Wildlife on Tuesday extended its fishing closure in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, and shellfish harvesting there remains closed by the state health department. Don't eat anything caught there, and keep kids and pets away from any oil on the shoreline.

Quiet skies. There have been no new drone reports since late September. The FBI's investigation into the earlier reports continues. As always, please don't post speculation about base security online.

Back home. Training aircraft have been returning from NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth since Sept. 20. If you live near the field, you've heard them. Some of you have written to say it's the best noise in town.
Self-care. Three weeks of boiling, hauling and cleaning take a toll on everyone. Military OneSource and your installation's family support programs offer free, confidential counseling. Take the help.
Have news from your unit, your street or your family readiness group? Send it in. We'll keep this space for you.

stories.headline: 'Tell us when': Calallen waits on pump parts that are coming the long way
stories.dek: Neighbors of the O.N. Stevens plant are nearing three weeks of boiling water. Leticia Ramos, who runs her street's water runs, says the delay is easier to take than the silence was.
body: The clipboard by Leticia Ramos' front door has a new column.
Next to the house numbers and the columns for "has car" and "needs help lifting," the Calallen schoolteacher has added one more: "Heard anything?"
"Everybody asks me if I've heard anything," said Ramos, 45. "Like I've got a direct line to the plant. I don't. I've got a clipboard."

Ramos lives a few minutes from the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, the city's only treatment plant. Since Sept. 18, when the citywide boil-water notice was issued, she has organized her street's water runs. This week the city said replacement parts for the plant's damaged pumps are delayed: the supplier, Delta Pumps & Controls, had its local warehouse flood in the same storm, and the parts are shipping from out of state.
Ramos said the news did not surprise her street. What stood out was that someone finally explained why.
"I'll be honest. I liked that they said it," she said. "A warehouse flooded. Okay. That's a reason. That's something I can tell the lady next door. 'Soon' is not a reason."

Teresa Gallegos, the utility's spokeswoman, said the city knows the wait is long. "We hear Calallen, and we hear everyone," Gallegos said. "We will keep telling people what we know, as soon as we know it. And we won't lift the notice until the water is tested and safe."

Ramos is practical about what comes next. The notice will be lifted, she said, and then people will forget what it was like. She wants the city to remember. "Write down what broke and how long it took," she said. "Then fix it so the next teacher doesn't have to do this with a clipboard."
In the meantime, the routine continues. At dusk the garden wagon rolls out again: two jugs for the older couple, a case for the corner house with the baby.
"That baby is going to grow up thinking water comes from a pot," Ramos said.

stories.headline: Oil in the marsh, supper off the table: what scientists will watch as the bays recover
stories.dek: The bays stay closed to fishing more than three weeks after the spill. An oceanographer explains what recovery looks like, and a pastor explains what the closure means for families who fish to eat.
body: At low tide, the edge of a Nueces Bay marsh tells the story in layers: green cordgrass on top, a dark band on the stems where the oil rode in on the surge, gray mud below.

"The marsh keeps a diary," said Dr. Nathan Brooks, a coastal oceanographer at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi. "That dark band is the entry for Sept. 14. Our job now is to read the next pages: how fast it fades, where it lingers, and what it does to the things that live there."

Oil from the Inner Harbor spill, an estimated 9,000 barrels released from two tankers as Hurricane Rafael closed in, spread across about 33 square miles of Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. Cleanup crews have worked the shorelines with boom since winds dropped, and the state opened a hotline for oiled wildlife. On Tuesday, Texas Parks and Wildlife extended its fishing closure in both bays; shellfish harvesting stays shut by order of the Texas Department of State Health Services.

Brooks said scientists will watch several things in the months ahead. Oil that settles into mud can break down slowly where oxygen is scarce. Marsh plants can recover if their roots survive. And shrimp, crabs and fish that grow up in the marshes are the link between the bay's health and people's kitchens. "Seafood testing is the bridge between the science and the dinner table," he said. "That's what will drive reopening."

He was careful about timelines. "Some places will look normal long before they are normal," Brooks said. "And some will look worse than they are. I'd rather say 'we'll know more after testing' than guess."

For some families near the bay, the closure isn't about sport. Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who runs a relief hub from her church fellowship hall in a low-income neighborhood near the water, said many of her neighbors fish from piers and seawalls to stretch the grocery budget.

"You'd be surprised how many suppers in this neighborhood used to start with a bucket and a cast net," Whitfield said. "Now it's a can of something. People understand why. They don't want their babies eating oil. But it's one more thing that costs money they don't have."
She said the hall has added canned fish and beans to what it hands out. "If the bay can't feed us for a while, we'll feed each other," she said.

Brooks said he hopes long-term monitoring includes the places where people fish from shore. "The people on the seawall are the ones most likely to eat what they catch," he said. "They should be the first ones we're thinking about when we test."

stories.headline: Not yet: State asks FEMA for household aid as damage checks lag
stories.dek: Texas has asked FEMA to add aid for households in three coastal counties. Until FEMA decides, nobody can register. Near the bay, families are waiting.
body: At Pastor Gloria Whitfield's fellowship hall, the question comes every day: "Pastora, when can we sign up for FEMA?"
"Not yet," Whitfield, 59, tells them. "Nobody can sign up yet. I'd rather tell you the truth than tell you something nice."

Here's why. Texas has formally asked FEMA to add Individual Assistance, the program that helps households, to the federal disaster declaration for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. The declaration issued Sept. 18 covers debris removal and emergency protective measures. Help for families depends on joint damage assessments, and those are moving slowly.

"We've got people trying to look at houses on streets they still can't drive down, and near shorelines where the spill response controls who goes in," says Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "It's slow because it's big. That's the reason, not an excuse."

Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6, says the agency has the state's request. "When there's a decision, we'll announce it, and we'll tell people plainly how to apply," she says.

A few blocks from the hall, Rosa Elizondo, 38, has a bucket in her hallway catching a drip from the ceiling. A home health aide and mother of three, she rents a duplex near the bay. No car, no savings for repairs. Her landlord says soon.
"People think FEMA is like a store. You go, you ask, you get," Elizondo says. "Nobody told us it's more like the bus. First it has to come."
Advocates say families without savings feel the wait most. Whitfield is starting a new page in her penciled binder for neighbors who will need help applying once aid opens.
What to do now: Take photos of damage before you clean up. Keep every receipt. If you have insurance, file your claim now. And if anyone offers to sign you up for federal aid today, it's a scam.

stories.headline: Opinion: The bays will heal on their own clock. Fishing families need one they can read.
stories.dek: Extending the closure of Nueces and Corpus Christi bays is the right call for public health. It should come with a clear testing plan and a plain-language update schedule for the people who make their living on the water.
body: I paddle these bays when I'm not writing about them. Since the storm, I haven't wanted to.

Texas Parks and Wildlife was right to extend its fishing closure in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays on Tuesday, and the state health department is right to keep shellfish harvesting shut. Oil from the Inner Harbor spill, about 9,000 barrels by the Unified Command's estimate, spread across about 33 square miles of water after Hurricane Rafael's surge. Some of it is sitting in marsh mud and bay sediment where shrimp and crabs grow up. Nobody should be eating seafood from those waters until testing says it is safe.
But "until testing says it's safe" is not a plan a shrimper can take to the bank.

Huy Nguyen, the Aransas Pass shrimper I interviewed for Tuesday's story, put it as plainly as anyone could: tell me a number, and I can plan around a number. He is not asking those agencies to rush. He is asking them to show their work.

Here is what that could look like. The agencies responsible should publish what they are testing, where and how often. They should say what results would allow a partial reopening, and which parts of the bays are likely to come back first. They should update that information on a regular schedule, even when the update is "nothing has changed." And they should say it in plain English, Spanish and Vietnamese, at the docks and boat ramps, not only online.
None of that requires knowing exactly when the bays will reopen. It requires treating the people who fish them as partners rather than spectators.

The cause of the spill is still under investigation, and the claims center run for the tankers' owners is so far taking only cleanup and property claims. Fishing families shouldn't have to wait for their turn there to get the most basic thing a closure owes them: information.

Bay shrimpers started this season with a fair catch and thin margins. Now many are watching the fall slip away from a dock. The bays will heal on their own schedule, and science can't hurry it. But the people who depend on them shouldn't be left guessing.
The marsh keeps its own time. The agencies should keep a clock the rest of us can read.

stories.headline: Nearly four weeks in, the church hub settles in for the long haul
stories.dek: Pastor Gloria Whitfield's fellowship hall started as an emergency stopgap after Rafael. Now it runs on a schedule, with a sign-up sheet and a list of who still needs what.
body: The handwritten sign by the fellowship hall door has company. Two weeks ago it said only "Take what you need. Bring what you can." Now a second sign hangs under it, typed and laminated: "Water: Mon/Wed/Fri. Food boxes: Tue/Sat. Rides: ask Pastor."
"We graduated," Pastor Gloria Whitfield said Sunday. "We went from emergency to routine. Routine is harder, honestly. In an emergency, people show up. In a routine, you have to keep them showing up."

Whitfield, 59, had her church handing out food and water within days of Hurricane Rafael, and in some neighborhoods near the bay that help came before official distribution did. Residents of those neighborhoods have since reported waiting days for help after the storm. For many of them, the hall became the first stop.

Nearly four weeks later, the needs have shifted. The city's boil-water notice is still in effect, and replacement parts for the water plant's damaged pumps are delayed, so water remains the biggest request. But there are new ones: cleaning supplies for mold, box fans, help reading insurance letters, rides to appointments. With bay fishing still closed, the hall has added canned fish and beans to its food boxes.

The volunteers have shifted too. Many who came the first week have gone back to work. A smaller crew keeps the place running: retirees, teenagers in the afternoons, and Rosa Elizondo, a home health aide who first came for water and now helps sort donations on her days off.
"Pastora gave me water when I needed it," Elizondo said. "Now I give two hours. That's the deal. Nobody wrote it down, but that's the deal."

Whitfield still keeps her penciled binder: names, addresses, needs, check marks. It is longer than it was, not shorter. "Some people are fine now and some people are worse," she said. "The ones who are worse are the ones with no car, no family nearby and a landlord who isn't answering. That's who we chase."
She said she would hand the list to anyone official who asks. "I'd give it to them today," she said. "Somebody come get it. I'll even make you a plate."
The early service started at 9. The sermon was short. The sign-up sheet was long.

stories.headline: Analysis: What Rafael has cost the Coastal Bend so far, by the numbers that are public
stories.dek: Four weeks after landfall, there is no official dollar estimate of the storm's damage. But the public figures already show where the region's economy is hurting, and for how long.
body: There is no official price tag yet on Hurricane Rafael, and there won't be for months. But four weeks after the storm came ashore on Mustang Island, the public numbers already show where the Coastal Bend economy is hurting, and for how long.

The port. The Corpus Christi Ship Channel has been closed to all traffic since Sept. 13, the day before landfall, and crude exports have been halted since the port shut to inbound ships a day earlier. The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports, by analysts' estimates. That means a month of the region's biggest export business on hold, along with the pilots, tug crews, terminal workers and truckers who depend on it.

"Every week the channel is closed is a week of revenue that doesn't come back," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Buyers find other barrels. Some of that business returns when the channel opens, but the lost weeks are lost."

The bays. Fishing and shellfish harvesting have been closed in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays since Sept. 18, after oil from the Inner Harbor spill, an estimated 9,000 barrels, spread across about 33 square miles of water. Texas Parks and Wildlife extended its fishing closure Oct. 5, and the state health department's shellfish closure stands. Shrimpers, guides and bait shops are absorbing the loss with no reopening date.

The water. The citywide boil-water notice has been in effect since Sept. 18, and replacement parts for the water plant's damaged pumps are delayed. Restaurants, coffee shops, child care centers and any business that runs on tap water are paying for workarounds: bottled water, ice and extra labor.

The cleanup. Two emergency contracts have entered the public record: Nueces County's $14.2 million sole-source debris removal contract with Vantorra Restoration LLC, and a $2.1 million federal emergency fuel contract for NAS Corpus Christi with Quellmar Fuel Partners. Those are costs to taxpayers, and they also put crews and trucks to work.

The land. About 43 square miles across Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties flooded, according to satellite imagery. Every flooded home is a repair bill, and for many families, a gap between what insurance pays and what rebuilding costs.

The strain. At the peak, 911 calls hit about 2,900 a day, nearly ten times normal, and emergency room visits for stomach illness ran about 180% above normal. Those numbers carry no dollar sign, but they show up later as overtime, missed work and medical bills.
What's missing: estimates of insured and uninsured losses, a count of businesses closed and timelines for the channel and the bays. Those will define the recovery more than any number above.

stories.headline: Stomach illness has eased, but the boil-water notice still matters
stories.dek: More than three weeks into the citywide notice, health officials urge residents not to let routines slip, especially in kitchens, child care settings and homes with babies or older adults.
body: Emergency rooms are no longer crowded with stomach-illness patients the way they were in late September. Health officials say that is exactly when people start to get careless.

"This is the dangerous part of a long boil-water notice," said Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District. "The emergency feels over. People get tired. They rinse a baby bottle under the tap, or they use tap water in the coffee maker because they think it gets hot enough. That's how cases come back."

Stomach illness visits began to ease in late September after a surge that pushed emergency room visits about 180% above normal and filled hallway beds. Wastewater testing, which first signaled norovirus in the city Sept. 20, helped officials track the spread.

The citywide boil-water notice, issued Sept. 18, remains in effect. The city said last week that replacement pump parts for the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant are delayed and shipping from out of state. No date has been set to lift the notice.
Shah's reminders for the long haul:
Coffee makers, refrigerator water dispensers and ice makers don't make tap water safe. Use boiled or bottled water, and turn off automatic ice makers.
Rinse fruits and vegetables with boiled or bottled water.
Wash dishes in a dishwasher with a hot drying cycle, or by hand with a final rinse in water with a small amount of unscented bleach added.
Bathe babies and toddlers with boiled water that has cooled, or give them sponge baths, so they don't swallow tap water. Adults can shower but should keep their mouths closed.
Give pets boiled or bottled water too.
Keep washing hands with soap and boiled or bottled water. Hand sanitizer is not enough against norovirus.
"Nobody gets a medal for the last week of a boil-water notice," Shah said. "But that's the week we find out whether people kept at it."

stories.headline: Port Aransas bait shop owner: 'Down to the studs. Customers next.'
stories.dek: Four weeks after Rafael gutted his shop near the jetties, Bill Hargrove has bare studs and plenty of stories, but not many customers.
body: PORT ARANSAS — The sign out front of Hargrove Bait & Tackle still says "OPEN-ISH." Inside, the walls are stripped to the studs, with Bill Hargrove's pencil notes scrawled across the bare wood.

"That's where the freezer goes. That's where the rods go. That's where the photo board goes, once people start catching fish again," Hargrove, 64, says, pointing. "I'm writing it on the wall so I don't forget. At my age, if it's not on the wall, it's not happening."

Hurricane Rafael's surge gutted the shop near the jetties when the storm came ashore Sept. 14. Hargrove spent the next weeks tearing out what the water ruined. Now he's planning how it all goes back, one wall at a time.

What hasn't come back is the crowd. Before the storm, Port Aransas had a strong summer, and bait shops and charters stayed busy. Now the island is quiet. Texas Parks and Wildlife has closed fishing in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays because of the oil spill, and it extended the closure last week.

"People call and ask, 'Bill, is it open?' and I tell them the truth," Hargrove says. "Then they ask about the jetties, and I tell them to check with Parks and Wildlife before they go. I'm a bait man, not a lawyer."
He's been selling ice, tackle and coffee, and listening a lot. "Half my business right now is therapy," he says. "Guy comes in for a pack of hooks and stays forty minutes to tell me about his roof."
He's optimistic, in his way. "The fish are still out there. The jetties are still out there. I'm still out here," he says. "Two out of three ain't bad. Three out of three, give it time."

stories.headline: Recovery checklist: what's still closed and what's changed, a month after Rafael
stories.dek: The boil-water notice, the bay fishing closure and the ship channel closure are still in place. Here's where things stand and what to do.
body: It's been almost a month since Hurricane Rafael came ashore on Mustang Island on Sept. 14. Here's where things stand as of Wednesday.

Water: STILL BOIL. The Sept. 18 citywide boil-water notice has not been lifted. Replacement parts for the O.N. Stevens plant's damaged pumps are delayed because the supplier's local warehouse flooded, and they're shipping from out of state. No date has been set to lift the notice.
Stomach illness: EASING. ER visits eased in late September after a surge. Keep up the handwashing, with soap and boiled or bottled water.

Bay fishing: CLOSED. Texas Parks and Wildlife extended its fishing closure in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays on Oct. 5, and the state health department's shellfish closure stays in place. Don't fish or harvest there, and avoid any oil on shorelines.
Ship channel: CLOSED. The Corpus Christi Ship Channel has been closed since Sept. 13, and crude exports are halted. No reopening date has been announced.

Spill investigation: ONGOING. The Coast Guard says investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo systems of the two tankers involved in the spill. A maintenance vendor says its remote-maintenance credentials were misused and that it revoked all remote access.
Debris: CONTRACT AWARDED. Nueces County awarded a $14.2 million emergency debris contract. Sort piles at the curb, out of the street, and check county channels for routes.
Scams: WATCH OUT. A researcher tied post-storm rumor posts to a lookalike aid site, aid-help-portal.example, also used in phishing emails. Don't click it.
Lights over the air station: QUIET. No new drone sightings since late September. The FBI's investigation continues.
Share this list with a neighbor who isn't online.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi channel closure passes one month; port says it is ready when the Coast Guard is
stories.dek: Crude exports from the nation's largest crude export port have been halted since Sept. 12. Port officials say berths and terminals will move as soon as the Coast Guard clears the channel.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — A month after the Coast Guard shut the Corpus Christi Ship Channel ahead of Hurricane Rafael, crude exports from the Port of Corpus Christi were still halted Wednesday.

The port, which handles about half of U.S. crude exports according to analysts' estimates, has had no export traffic through the channel since Sept. 12. At the anchorage east of Port Aransas, 14 vessels were waiting when the port closed to inbound ships that day.

"We are ready when the Coast Guard is," port spokesperson Javier Salinas said. "Our job is to have berths, pilots and terminals lined up so the minute the channel opens, ships move. That work is happening now."

Salinas declined to give a reopening date, noting that port conditions are set by the Coast Guard, which has said the channel will reopen when it is safe for traffic. Spill response continues in the Inner Harbor and the bays, where about 9,000 barrels released by two moored tankers spread across about 33 square miles after the storm.

Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics, said traders are focused on what comes after the reopening as much as on the reopening itself. "The first day isn't the story. The story is how fast the backlog clears," she said. "You've got ships that have been waiting offshore and buyers who have been sourcing elsewhere for a month. It will take time to get back to rhythm."

Holloway said the Coast Guard's investigation into possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo systems of the two tankers is also on traders' minds. "Nobody's pricing it in yet," she said. "But everyone's asking their own terminals what's connected to what."
The Coast Guard has not announced when the channel will reopen.
